#4005. The Blood Of Dawnwalker Just Got A Free 1.2 Update, Adding New Game Plus

The Blood of Dawnwalker is one of the year's biggest, most ambitious games, and the developers over at Rebel Wolves have done a good job cleaning up bugs and performance issues in the weeks since launch. Today, that trend continued; the new 1.2 update is out now on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC, and it adds New Game Plus.

The new mode is uniquely ideal for a game like Dawnwalker. The narrative is very player-driven, whether it has to do with your literal dialogue options, your ability to manage your vampiric hunger, or the order you complete quests, and all of these elements can cause your experience to vary wildly. It makes sense, then, that players would want to jump back in to try things again and see what might happen if the game is played differently, and New Game Plus allows them to do that while keeping combat fresh.

According to the update notes on the Dawnwalker website, "NG+ unlocks after you complete the game’s Epilogue and lets you experience the story again while keeping your progress – mainly your character level, skills, and inventory." You don't gain access to these skills until you complete the prologue, however, which marks the adventure's proper start.

The new mode will also rebalance the world's level scaling. In the base game, certain areas are much harder than others, but in New Game Plus, all enemies will rise in power to match your level, meaning you can explore the world in whatever order you want. On that note, the level cap has also been raised to 100, and protagonist Coen can collect new, more powerful versions of weapons marked with an "NG+" label.

That's basically everything in this update. Rebel Wolves also added some slight tweaks to combat in the base game and adjusted some geometry in the open world, but the main focus here was New Game Plus. This is in contrast to the 1.1 update, which added a much wider suite of bug fixes and made the game run more smoothly.

#4004. Rockstar’s Rob Nelson Explains Why You Can’t Wield GTA 6's Chainsaws

GTA 6 is being celebrated for more reasons every day, and rightfully so. However, the most striking thing about the game, since it’s the first thing you see and it’s hitting you over the head every second you’re looking at it, is how stunning it is. That realism is one of the reasons why the option to make Jason and Lucia hyper-violent is taken out of the player’s hands.

Rockstar producer Rob Nelson revealed the level of thinking that went into not only some of the endless things you can do in Leonida, but also some of the things you can’t in an interview with VGC. One of the things Nelson discussed was the decision to not include weapons that would allow for a heightened level of violence that have been present in previous GTA entries, like chainsaws and katanas.

Despite a mountain of leaks, Rockstar managed to keep one of GTA 6’s biggest plot points a secret throughout all of its development.

“As far as the chainsaw – I think it would have been too much for this game at this resolution and these characters,” Nelson explains, adding, “It’s not a resource thing.” Other omissions, such as not being able to play games like darts or bowling, were confirmed to have been left on the cutting room floor because Rockstar simply didn’t think it was worth the time and effort when those resources could be put to better use elsewhere.

The realism that you get with GTA 6 means even standard stuff that has to be in the games, like shooting someone or hitting them with a blunt object, is far more visceral than it has ever been before. When coupled with how much more grounded GTA 6’s lead characters are, giving them the option to carve someone up with a chainsaw just doesn’t fit.

“Even at the most psycho, did Jason and Lucia really need that – what’s that going to look like?” Nelson continues, adding, “You’re always trying to find what is the right sort of line and the right balance, it really just depends, you want to feel like you can interact with as much of the world as possible,” when asked about chainsaws existing in Leonida, but Rockstar choosing not to let players interact with them at all.

It’s a tricky line to walk. A huge part of GTA has always been about players doing whatever they like, and going “psycho,” as Nelson puts it. Once I was done with GTA San Andreas's story, I input cheats to give pedestrians weapons and then made them riot. The whole point of that game for me after that was for it to be as chaotic and unrealistic as possible.

That was a long time ago. Sure, GTA has always been violent, but its violence has never been realised with the same realism as it is in GTA 6. Not just the way it looks, but the way you play and the repercussions that come along with everything you do. Jason and Lucia are the closest the series has ever seen to protagonists that act like real people. They’re not caricatures like the leads in previous GTA games. They might be criminals, but as Nelson says, they’re not psychos who are going to fight their way out of a situation with a chainsaw. It wouldn’t make sense for them, and it no longer makes sense for GTA.

A new Love and Deepspace banner event is here with a lot of rewards to earn, and brand-new Memories for all five lads to unlock.

Love and Deepspace has kicked off the next big in-game moment and is celebrating Chinese New Year with the arrival of a new 5-Star Memory Series. This year's spring-themed banner is available now until February 27, and it comes with a host of events.

The Mortality’s Tenderness banner features five new limited-time 5-Star Memories, one each for the game’s five love interests. The theme is all about warmth, reunion, and intimacy, taking place in a Wuxia-inspired setting that's once again an alternate universe from the main story of the game.

The new memory cards are Xavier: Blades with Blossoms, Zayne: Entwined Kites, Rafayel: Carved Gemheart, Sylus: Shared Lanterns, and Caleb: Clearday Return. You can pick three of the five to focus on and further pick one to guarantee on your second 5-star pull; and you can earn wish rewards by making cumulative wishes over the course of the event.

Some of the rewards you could get include limited headwear, Limited Deepspace Wishes, and — of course — Memory-themed outfits and hairstyles inspired by the new Memories. Outside of wish rewards, the Memory Series comes with growth tasks that rewards you with in-game materials for levelling up the new cards during the event. When you reach Rank 1 for any new Memory from the banner, you’ll earn a Memory-themed outfit with a special colour that matches your chosen love interest.

Illusio returns as part of the new event, too, letting you customise the look of Kindled Moments across all five new Memories. Things you can customise include selecting the outfits and accessories for each love interest, so you can recreate Kindled Moments in your own style. As always, Kindled Moments will go back to their default look after the event ends.

There’s a new mini-game to play, too, available only during the event. It’s called Courteous Fare, a frantic but familiar restaurant management simulation that allows you to unlock a variety of rewards.

Furthermore, if you log in for 10 days throughout the event, you can unlock a new outfit set, Wealth Overflow, which can be worn by any of the love interests as well as the heroine. There are other login rewards, too, like 10 Deepspace Wishes, 10 Empyrean Wishes, His and My Outfit sets, two dynamic portrait photo poses, and loads more.

Finally, the Golden Fortune event adds even more daily log in rewards in the form of one free "shake" per day, from which you can earn a random reward of between 68 and 108 Diamonds — that adds up to a total of 1,296 Diamonds if you show up every day.

The new market home is, says Valve, faster to load up, but it's not just a new gloss of paint. You've also now got a watchlist that will let you keep track of various market items across multiple games. You can save specific items, a general item type, or even a particular search. I imagine this will be useful to those of you who play the Steam market like an '80s Wall Street guy shouting into a big phone.

The biggest change for me personally—that's why people read the news, for the biggest changes for me personally—is streamlined selling and relisting. You can now change the price of items you have listed for sale without laboriously taking them down and relisting them. You can just update the price tag and have done with it. Similarly, if you're selling directly from the Steam mobile app, you'll be able to approve those sales via a pop-up rather than navigating to the confirmation page. This is truly huge news for the weirdest guys you know (me).

All that aside, the market home page will now also track your in-progress badges, and search results now have a list view. There are a few more new things, but Valve confined them to an 'and finally' set of bulletpoints, so here they are in their original bulletpoint form.

#4000. Civilization Developer Firaxis Lays Off A Third Of Its Staff

Firaxis, the studio behind the Civilization series, has laid off around 60 employees, representing a third of its staff. The report comes from Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier.

In a statement provided to Bloomberg by a spokesperson from 2K, a subsidiary of Firaxis' owner, Take-Two, “Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.”

In addition to the 60 affected staffers, Firaxis studio head Heather Hazen is also departing. Bloomberg also reports, via anonymous Firaxis employees speaking to the outlet, that the studio is working on an unannounced XCOM game that has had a challenging development, with the team recently missing an important development milestone. This project, if it releases, will be the first Firaxis-developed XCOM game since XCOM: Chimera Squad in 2020.

Firaxis’ most recent release is Civilization VII, which launched in February 2025 to favorable reviews but initially "slow" sales, according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick last August.  The game currently has a Mixed reception on Steam after Firaxis spent the last year updating the game to address player complaints. Before Civilization VII, Firaxis shipped Marvel's Midnight Suns in 2022, another critically well-received game that failed to meet sales expectations.

"I've always wanted to try, even if I fail, to change things"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Plenty of people would have told you that the real-time strategy game began to 'die out' in the late 2000s, a once-mighty genre that no longer interested modern audiences. But the more nuanced version of that narrative is that the RTS evolved, various core ideas stripped of their outside complexities before being expanded into their own genres. Without Warcraft 3, for instance, there wouldn't have been a League of Legends or Dota 2. Now, a leading figure behind another 'dying' genre says that its DNA is simply to be found elsewhere - primarily within the RPG.

Speaking to Edge, legendary immersive sim designer Warren Spector said that "the heart of the immersive sim has kind of been adopted by mainstream gaming." Best known for series like Thief, System Shock, Ultima, and Deus Ex, Spector is widely considered a major force in the development of the entire imsim genre, and that influence is a major personal marker of success.

"One of my egomaniacal success criteria was to have influence. I've always wanted to try, even if I fail, to change things." His argument, however, is that he has very much not failed to change things, and that the ideas that were once the individual domain of the immersive sim are now found much further afield.

"I don't think you can look at Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom and not see a little bit of Deus Ex in it," he says. "And I think roleplaying games now are far more immersive sim-y than they used to be, going further to empower players to tell their own stories." While the two Zelda titans are obvious examples, other RPGs have also done work to deserve that mantle - Baldur's Gate 3 is a particularly good example of the imsim's systems-driven heritage, and a lot of what we're hearing about GTA 6 implies that some of its big ideas - particularly its Wanted system - will be very immersive.

The result, for Spector, is that a trace of the old self exists in the new self. Even if immersive sims aren't a driving force in the industry right now, he says, "I don't know that we're dead. I think we're like a parasite that's invaded the body. And that's all you can ask for. Making games different and better and more what they should be, and empowering players to become authors - that's all I ever wanted to do, and now there are lots of people doing that, even if they don't realise they are."

#3997. Grand Theft Auto VI Review - Outrageous Fortune

Many superlatives will be heard in the discussion around Grand Theft Auto VI – biggest world, most activities, best graphics, deepest narrative – but its real triumph is the way all those features and others work in service of a cohesive, believable immersion in a criminal fantasy that is hard to grasp until you’ve played it for yourself.

Rockstar’s latest returns players to a dramatically expanded version of the Vice City seen in a prior game, now largely unrecognizable after real and in-game years have passed. Leonida is a joy to explore, filled with a wealth of activities, both mundane and illicit. The game’s design makes many ordinary tasks as compelling as the illegal ones. Go fishing off the boat, brew coffee to wake up, work out at the gym, scuba dive for long-lost treasure, dust crops, motocross in the mud, go dancing at the club. As you move between those activities, the world feels alive with minor events, from traffic accidents to shady individuals a little too interested in your walk to the ATM. GTAVI delights in life's minutiae, with animations, voice lines, and background characters that keep things fresh even dozens of hours into the story. The level of detail everywhere is astounding and, at times, overwhelming. Getting sidetracked is easy.

The focus on detail carries into the visuals. Lucia’s hair blows in the wind, and she absently pushes it back behind her ear. A drug den is littered with paraphernalia and empty containers. A shifty contact quirks a smile – your only hint that things are about to go south. Sweat glistens on your character’s skin after a hard workout, their breathing and heart rate noticeably heightened. Clouds roll together in the sky, creating realistic weather simulations. The commitment to an authentic simulated world is encompassing, thoughtful, and intentional, a testament to hand-crafted and meticulously painstaking development work, paying off in an absorbing play-space that is hard to step away from.

While the day-to-day simulation is fascinating, it also adds pacing and counterpoint to the explosive march of major missions, narrative threads, and set-piece encounters that drive the game forward. Not even one of these meticulously choreographed sequences deserves to be spoiled; they run the gamut from amusing shenanigans at a strip club to intense chases and escapes fueled by raging gunfights and explosions. Many of the best moments leverage an expert sense of musical accompaniment, weaving a slick original score alongside one of the most impressive and wide-ranging licensed soundtracks ever heard in a video game – often to surprisingly emotional effect.

Ranged combat is punchy and enjoyable; smart use of cover and time-slowing focus makes most battles manageable. On-foot navigation is in a similar boat – simple to pick up and uninterested in needless complexity or challenge; the focus is on choosing smart moments for stealth, knowing when to run and when to fight, and selecting the precise instant for a burst of sudden action. Driving is fast and intense, made more appealing by a huge variety of functionally distinct vehicles to enjoy. If there’s a fault to the core and optional story missions, it’s that many feel a bit on rails regarding where to go and what to do at each step. At the same time, that directed approach keeps the pace relentless, and the action and outcomes thrilling. Over many hours, the game morphs and throws new wrenches into the mix at key junctures, teasing and then playing out criminal experiences from petty theft to group heists to illicit spec ops, and punctuates those distinct vibes with memorable and singular moments.

Like its predecessors, GTAVI simultaneously lampoons and celebrates life in modern America, taking aim at targets like social media, wellness lifestyles, rap and music culture, manosphere content, and dozens more. The caricatures land so well because, in many cases, they’re (sadly) barely over the line of the absurdity we see reflected in real life, and because Rockstar so ably captures individual subcultures, dialects, and situations. Behind it all is a scathing critique of wealth inequality and the inherent unfairness of a system that sets most up to fail. It’s a bitter message delivered in honey-wrapped, exhilarating gameplay, but it shines through.

Of all its significant feats, the relationship between Lucia and Jason elevates the game to new heights, lending this installment a heart, tension, and emotional core missing from prior entries. This is, without a doubt, video gaming’s most richly drawn and compelling romance, featuring two leads who are immediately relatable and compelling to watch. Player actions dictate the strength of their bond, deepening the sense of engagement. Like the best crime fiction, you’re left surprised by how much you cheer for two people who regularly commit terrible acts. The two collectively suffer the slings and arrows of a world that always seems stacked against them; the fortune they amass is not a power grab, but a desperate attempt to cling to each other and come out the other side together, and the player can’t help but cheer them on and dread how fate might stand in the way.

Grand Theft Auto VI is a generational game that stands toe-to-toe with many of the great crime stories and satires across other media. It showcases both the entertainment value of interactive play and the current high-water mark for technical and artistic detail in games. Hunt for and count up all the minor faults or foibles you like, but then note how you just spent another hour lost in this remarkable escape into criminality, wanton violence, egregious sex, and the elusive potential of true love.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

Season 2 of Battlefield 6 looks to bring a host of broad, positive changes to XP, progression, audio and more.

Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the new content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a big new map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

The real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the new season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

Audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

The first Switch 2 jailbreaks arrived just over a month ago, and we've already reached Nintendo's nightmare scenario: dumped games can now be played on hacked consoles. That means the door to piracy on the console is already swinging wide open, and if history is any indication it's going to be very difficult for Nintendo or its lawyers to get it closed again.

A hacker called Olmectron has released a tool called nx2-relink, which can be used to turn a Switch 2 game dump into a homebrew program that can run on a jailbroken console. As noted by hacking and homebrew site GTAtemp, this is an early and experimental piece of software, so compatibility is limited right now and you will run a risk of bricking your console by using it.

Strictly speaking, there's nothing illegal in using the tool as advertised, making backups of games you own and have dumped yourself, though any jailbroken console risks a ban from online services by Nintendo. Olmectron says the tool includes "no games, no keys and no Nintendo files, and it won't get them for you." But, as far as I can tell, there's nothing preventing you from using this newfound power to simply download other people's dumps and use them on your console – which is the very definition of piracy.

nx2-relink features heavy contributions from Claude, as with many recent breakthroughs in the console hacking and homebrew scene. AI is dramatically increasing the pace at which developers can break through console security measures, and this isn't even the only Switch 2 backup tool to appear in the past 24 hours. A separate dev demonstrated a console booting a dumped version of Donkey Kong Bananza just yesterday, "opening the flood gates" to a new era of Switch 2 hacks.

And, well, yes – the flood gates do seem to be wide open, and this trickle of dumping tools is likely a warning for the absolute tsunami of Switch 2 piracy that's likely to follow.

#3993. Congratulations to people who feel mean shooting random NPCs, because GTA 6 tries "to provide mechanisms that encourage" empathy

When you think about GTA as a series, the first thing that probably comes to mind is driving through crowds of people, gunning down whoever you like, just generally doing crime without any care in the world. I wouldn't exactly call it an empathy game, not to say that other games are any better at such a thing anyway. But with GTA 6 out, crikey, next bloody week, a new interview has gone up with co-studio head Rob Nelson where he shared that you have a bit more space to be empathetic compared to previous entries.

"Crime is a fundamental part of GTA - at least up until now, it has been," Nelson told The Guardian (via @GameRoll_, ta IGN) in a new interview. "We're trying to make sure we're not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out." When asked about whether this will be the first GTA game to encourage people to be empathetic, Nelson responded, "I would say so. I would say that it's a product of the story we're trying to tell. We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to."

I am deeply curious as to what those mechanics may be, given that most of what we've seen so far is pretty relegated to shootin', lootin' and a bit of smoochin'. If you steal a car, is there an NPC that loses their job because of it? Can you repair the harm you caused through that action? I'm sure hardly anyone else that's vibrating through their skin in excitement for almost having the game in their fingertips will be asking such questions, I'm just often wary of empathy mechanics in games.

In any case, doesn't matter all that much for us PC lot just yet, especially because Rockstar are preparing themselves both legally and technically to tackle pirated copies of the game. Rockstar will obviously be quite busy at the moment too, not just because of that whole launching a game thing, but because UK-based workers will be voting to unionise as we speak. If formed, it could be 1600 members strong, which would make it the biggest games union in the UK. Solidarity with all the workers as the voting process continues. I hope you get the result you deserve.

World of Warcraft: Forever's absolutely had me enthralled, as per my review (and about 220+ hours of my actual life), but that's not to say there aren't issues. Over the weekend and going on into this week, Blizzard's had to play whack-a-mole with both exploits and what appears to be a long-standing bug affecting one of the tanking classes' core mechanics.

First, those exploits—players discovered that lockboxes contained a sort of quantum loot, in that the actual roll of the lockboxes seemed tied to the player peeking inside of them, rather than what was inside regardless. If you turned off auto-loot, you can open a lockbox without actually pulling the loot into your bag. Then, if you sent that lockbox to another player via mail, they'd get something different.

Essentially, players could simply play a game of mass pass-the-parcel to ensure favorable lockbox results, further busting up the economy after the Blackmaw Hold drama earlier this month. That's since been hotfixed, simply disabling the mechanic, with a more elegant solution to come further down the road: "Today, we’re working on a proper fix that restores the ability to peek and partially loot lockboxes, and makes them otherwise work as intended."

Meanwhile, the Obsidian Sentinel in Uldaman was briefly rendered lootless. As spotted by WoWHead, players could hop into the dungeon and repeatedly rinse the boss to grab a cheeky 18 or so gold in 15 minutes by vendoring the loot as a max-level character.

While that's not really game-breaking (instance lockouts are limited to five per hour), if you had an organised group of level 60s all funnelling gold to the same guy—like, say, if you were a streamer with a dedicated fanbase that didn't mind wasting a quarter of an hour, or if you were a large-scale RMT operation—there's a bigger problem.

That lootless state turned out to be a band-aid, as Blizzard simply lowered the vendor costs later.

Perhaps the biggest hiccup over the past weekend, though, is the fact that Sunder Armor (and other armor-reducing effects like faerie fire) very well might just not do anything. I hopped in-game to test it on my warrior and saw no noticeable difference between Sunder Armor in both dungeons and the overworld while fighting lower level targets, though my testing capabilities were limited solo, since armor is affected by the level of whoever's attacking the target: And if I rock up to an on-level elite in a dungeon at 60, I tend to die before I can get a good sample.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Fortunately, I don't need to be too thorough. There's a lot more comprehensive math and log-testing on this github post: "Once an armor debuff goes on, players' and pets' hits barely move, same as the report says. About 5% of the armor drop actually shows up in the damage, and more stacks don't help." The evidence is all pretty convincing.

While those other exploits are annoying oopsies, arguably just a result of players—who find edge cases like water finds cracks—stress-testing the system? The Sunder Armor bug is sort of huge, since that's one of the protection warrior's main group utilities (aside from being a tanky meatshield). It still appears to be filling its primary role of threat generation, but: Yikes.

There's no mention of it in the hotfixes, but I'll update this article if one pops up in the coming days.

#3991. Diablo 4’s next class is the Warlock, but you can sort of play it today in Diablo 2: Resurrected’s new DLC

Blizzard has officially unveiled the Warlock, the second class coming to Diablo 4 with Lord of Hatred.

Diablo 4’s segment in the big Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight was among the biggest, even if the reason most of us tuned in was somewhat spoiled earlier in the same livestream. Blizzard unveiled the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.

The Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords. The Warlock is the edgy, antihero counterpart to the Paladin’s purity and devotion to the Light.

The livestream did not show off any Warlock gameplay, but Blizzard is planning a dedicated livestream to show off the new class’ gameplay, and dig deeper into its lore and abilities. That show is scheduled for March 5.

What we did get to see was our first look at Skovos, the expansion’s new region. This Mediterranean-inspired location is where the new story arc will unfold, but it’s also being positioned as the endgame destination for Diablo 4 once the credits roll.

Lord of Hatred, of course, as previously revealed, introduces two new endgame modes in War Plans, and Echoing Hatred.

War Plans lets you create a custom playlist of up to five endgame activities to target specific rewards and create your own experience. There’s a new activity tree that works with all endgame activities, and creating War Plans is how you earn progression there.

Echoing Hatred, on the other hand, is a rare event that pits you against legions of Mephisto’s minions. It’s triggered through a rare lootable item that unlocks access. It’s essentially horde mode; where you’ll face unending waves of enemies, though not without a couple of twists.

We also got a bit more colour on the expanded class skill trees, which all players will benefit from when the expansion arrives. The Talisman system, which unlocks set bonuses, was also shown off. And, of course, the return of the iconic Horadric Cube, which gives you control over Affixes.

The Anniversary Spotlight should’ve had a Year of the Warlock subtitle, because the class is also making its way to both Diablo Immortal, as well as Diablo 2: Resurrected. The showcase revealed the Reign of the Warlock DLC, which adds the aforementioned Warlock to D2R - its first new class in 25 years.

Reign of the Warlock, which is available now in D2R, also makes a few updates to the game, such as new quality of life features, the Colossal Ancients endgame encounter, updated Terror Zones and more. You also get some cosmetics in Diablo 4 if you purchase this expansion.

You can replace Dark Souls with Bloodborne or Elden Ring, I've typically just been a coward when it comes to the idea of fighting another, real person. They're probably going to be better than me! I don't use tactics in Souls games, I use brute force until I get my way! That being said, I do have to admit I quite like the look of Rasen, a game that is essentially just the PvP component of Dark Souls (or PvE if you just want to take on some computer-controlled enemies) that just launched into early access.

To say that it is just straight up Dark Souls combat would be unfair, from the looks of things. For one, it looks more like it leans a tad towards Sekiro with a blades-only kind of affair, whether that be big or small. And blades a plenty they have, ranging from your classic sword, to scythes, to halberds and all sorts. It's a much flashier looking affair too, with fancy slashing effects that seem to buff moves and a pace that seems much faster than Souls games tend to be.

You can take part in matches with up to eight people, which presumably extends to AI (not that kind) enemies too, in "atmospheric duels, clashes, deathmatches and more." It looks neat! And best of all, unusually for a 3D arena fighter, it has rollback netcode. For those unfamiliar, and to try and explain it simply, this is essentially a bit of tech you'll find in predominantly 2D fighting games that predicts every possible input you could make in a given moment, helping to reduce lag time and allow for tighter matches (and less rage quitting).

That's a bit harder to do in a 3D environment given that you have a lot more options at your disposal when it comes to movement, so if it works that's some impressive stuff! And we could all quite easily find out together, as a demo for Rasen is available to try out. Or, alternatively, you can just pick it up whole hog on Steam right now, as it's available in early access.

#3988. Forage and fight for ingredients in a magical 1960s Italy and whip up some tasty meals Cooking Mama style in The Snackbar at the End of the World

If a game is about cooking, at minimum I'll have to give it a quick testspin. Outside of this whole writing about video games thing, my other lot in life is soul bound to food, so I'm always curious to see how the two can be mixed together. And earlier this week, The Snackbar at the End of the World was revealed, a wonderfully cartoonish action-adventure game set in a magical, slightly post-apocalyptic version of 1960s Italy where you go out and forage for ingredients while fending off monstrous crops before turning them into tasty meals back in your struggling restaurant.

First up, I just have to gush over the artstyle a bit. The whole game is hand-drawn with a colourful, comic book look that has an impressive sense of depth to it. It gives off a deep love of Italian architecture and landscapes, and that admiration clearly extends to the food too. Once you've gotten the ingredients you need, you then, loosely in the vein of Cooking Mama, prepare them and make various classic Italian dishes by performing some quick minigames. Simple, but charming! The rest of the time you're off killing some ghoulies that look like mutated fruit and veggies, with the occasional fungus-possessed hog and, uh, haunted statues? I think?

I'm also quite pleased about two points made on the game's Steam page. First is the content description: "This game features cartoon violence, sensitive political themes set in a fictional world, and depictions of an oppressive government committing crimes against its citizens." There is clearly a romantic quality to the game and I'd be worried if it didn't acknowledge any of the political context of the decades preceding.

The other line reads, "Every sound effect, musical note, design decision, and line of code is human-made. Because this game is about human relationships and delicious food – and that’s not a story we would ever trust AI to tell." Thank the lord! Right now there's no release date attached to The Snackbar at the End of the World, unsurprising given it was only announced this week. But while we all wait for a date, you could perhaps join me in throwing it a wishlist on Steam.

#3986. Exclusive – Behind The Romance: Rockstar Talks GTAVI’s Jason And Lucia

After dozens of hours exploring Leonida, I have a lot of positive things to say about Grand Theft Auto VI, and shared as much in our review of the game. But for my part, the feature that elevated the game most prominently above Rockstar Games’ other (excellent) games wasn’t its graphics, missions, or action – it was the storytelling and interplay between the two lead protagonists. Jason and Lucia bring heart, emotional depth, and a sense of genuine threat to the crime fantasy, as you grow attached to them and start cheering for them against all the odds stacked against them.

We reached out to senior members of the Rockstar Games team to ask about their thoughts on Jason and Lucia, and this is what they had to share.

During my playthrough, the Jason and Lucia dynamic really elevated the experience, adding heart and emotional weight to the expected mix of action, driving, and activities around Leonida. Was a couple or romantic relationship the plan or goal for the game from very early on in development, or did that come later? Do you see the focus on Jason and Lucia’s relationship as one of the features that separates Grand Theft Auto VI from your prior work on storytelling in the game series?

Stephen Donkin, Vice President of Design: “The dual protagonists and the relationship between the two of them was there from very early in development, but exactly how that was expressed in the game did change over time. It was an enormous challenge for us to get them working together in the open world together and finding exactly how that would work. As we started to layer in more mechanics, dialogue, and incremental features across all teams, it just clicked at some point. The ability to be together in the open world also allowed us for new ways to tell the story of the game and to bring some of the exposition and narrative into the open world in a way we hadn’t been able to do before. Hearing these little bits of dialogue as you are just tooling around the world that have specific context to what you as a player have just been doing in the story really knits it all together.”

The player has a choice for how to develop the relationship between the two leads, but I imagine most players are drawn toward helping it thrive. In early playtests, is that what you observed?

Katie Pica, Design Director: Player Systems & Progression:“Overall, we’ve seen that players are invested in supporting Jason and Lucia’s relationship but we don’t favor a specific path through the game, it is completely down to player choice.”

It feels like a lot of the game’s driving narrative beats factor for a close connection between Jason and Lucia. Was it challenging to craft variations that included a more tense or distant connection between the two? Is that even possible?

Luke Howard, Senior Design Director: Missions & Visualization:“One of the core goals of this game was to tell the story of Jason and Lucia with a base line relationship where they are amicable, if just platonic, as they still share the same ultimate goals and need each other to achieve them. So, this gave us a good platform on the main flow to expand particularly intense or emotional moments they experience with variation that can expand on their romantic relationship, while not losing anything if that doesn’t exist. In short, we did develop variation in scenes and interactions that range from subtle to more significant, but done in a way that should feel authentic to the player’s choices, relationship-wise and also criminal profile.

One example is after Lucia helps Kordell’s gang pull off an intense armored truck robbery she shares the information with Raul’s crew. Afterwards Jason pulls Lucia aside to see how she's coping. This moment carries several variations where the performance direction was captured multiple ways to cover a range emotional energy between them. The actors deliveries are brilliant and nuanced – these small tender moments are where we tried to craft pieces that when added up together over the course of the story, author an authentic version of the player’s Jason and Lucia.”

Were there any fictional couples or real-life couples that the team looked at for inspiration in shaping the Jason and Lucia dynamic, whether those couples came from big crime stories or not?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“We definitely started by looking at all the “couple on the run” movies. There are a lot of them but the ones that we kept coming back to were Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway in Bonnie and Clyde, McQueen and MacGraw in The Getaway (the Jim Thomson book is also great), True Romance, Thelma and Louise. Clooney and JLo’s dynamic in Out of Sight, as well. And then a lot of buddy movies actually – Riggs and Murtaugh, Butch and Sundance, Mike Lowry and Marcus Burnett, etc. for their back and forth together. In terms of having a game where the characters can change based on how you play and whether you really lean into and enjoy the crime spree we thought about how both Pulp Fiction and Natural Born Killers start with a couple in a diner pulling out guns, but then how different those couples are and how different those scenarios play out. Jason and Lucia are a lot tougher than Tim Roth and Amanda Plummer but we liked the idea of telling a story where Jason and Lucia could end up being closer to either end of that spectrum based on what the player was doing.”

Sex and intimacy are notoriously complicated and challenging to present in games. How did you aim to strike a balance with their private moments together that felt authentic? Any thoughts about how or why it’s so challenging to present adult relationships in video games?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“This is definitely something we thought a lot about and spent a long time trying to get right. The actors who play Jason and Lucia were so good, and they had a natural chemistry and part of it was just trying to capture some of that.

There’s this trade off in making games between player control and then scripted scenarios. We try and give the player as much control as we can because we are working in an interactive medium and actually doing something rather than watching it is going to feel more powerful. But then you have the ability to really mess around and break the illusion of a tender or romantic moment or whatever it is. So the relationship aspect of this story is there if a player wants to engage in it, but if they don’t the story can play out differently.”

In its best moments of genuine support, regular connection, open communication, and flirty or engagement with one another, Jason and Lucia can come across as a pretty ideal model of good relationships – even while they’re simultaneously committing major crimes together. Was that juxtaposition of a healthy romantic relationship against an external world of illicit activity an explicit goal for how the narrative came together?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“That was the goal, yes. You are really living with these characters – they’re eating, sleeping, showering, throwing away their trash, or not. The relationship needed to feel real to sit alongside all of that. Then even just as a development team, we live with these characters for years and years. We wanted them to be people we could like, care about, and root for. And they needed to like each other. But then the world itself is so crazy and chaotic and seemingly on the brink of collapse.

When we set out to make this game, and go into that multiyear development marathon, we said we wanted to spend our time working on something with heart, and with some characters you could care about and root for. It’s barely worth even stating, but we are living in a time when people are divided along almost every line, and feelings about the future are pretty bleak. We wanted to create a world that held up a mirror to that, showed that fever pitch of craziness that we are all maybe a couple of bad decisions away from, but we wanted the story we were going to tell to have something positive at its core and the message that human connection is better than division.”

The game automatically moves you to play one character or another at certain points, but for many sequences, you can choose your playable lead. In your experience playing and watching others play, do most players gravitate toward one character or another as “their character?”

Stephen Donkin, Vice President of Design:“It really varied in our playthroughs. They are both such great characters and performances that people seemed to gravitate to both of them in different ways. But overall, we have found the split of time between characters to be relatively even on a per-playthrough and also at a macro level.”

The first HBO Lego Harry Potter sets have been revealed, and they're remaking some classic kits... but fans aren't all enthused by the result.

After being teased earlier this year, the initial wave of Lego Harry Potter kits based on HBO's new series revisits some old haunts; the lineup includes the Gryffindor Common Room, the Hogwarts Express, and Privet Drive. These include new designs and minifigures based on the TV show, but there are obviously similarities to what we've seen before – and that seems to be a sticking point for some. In a Reddit post discussing the sets, the top comment notes that they "they look like bootlegs of the originals lol."

While there's positive feedback as well (particularly toward Privet Drive's faux-Tudor design), I'm finding just as many negative responses on social media after a quick look through the likes of Instagram. These sets are clearly dividing the community, and I can't imagine it's the reception Lego was hoping for. Here are the kits themselves:

The Gryffindor Common Room is a constant throughout the Potter stories, so it makes sense that Lego would remake it here in its new HBO form. This one is made up of 738 pieces, comes with five minifigures (Harry, Ron, Hermione, Parvati, and Lavender), as well as lots of little details on almost every surface.UK: £79.99 at Lego

This is probably the most unique of the sets, as the faux-Tudor exterior is quite different from the old movie version. The kit has 545 pieces and four minifigs to go with a brick-built '90s car – Harry, Uncle Vernon, Aunt Petunia, and Dudley. UK: £54.99 at Lego

What with Harry's first trip to Hogwarts being such a pivotal moment in the story, it makes sense that the Hogwarts Express would feature as a major new set. This is just the latest in a long line of models recreating this train, and while the engine itself is practically identical, the HBO version of the platform looks like it includes a little cafe waiting area that we've not seen before.UK: £89.99 at Lego

The final set to be revealed thus far is a BrickHeadz kit, recreating characters in a larger scale. This one has Harry, Malfoy, and Hagrid presumably while they're wandering the Forbidden Forest in detention. It's made up of 380 pieces.UK: £22.99 at Lego

#3984. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

While following a peculiar trail of silver and saffron leaves around the largest roots of the Treehouse, you come across a hexagonal wooden door lying half-hidden among ivy and moss. Scraping away the dirt, you discover a faint, absurd engraving of a newspaper. What mystery is here? You turn the brass knob – strange, it is warm! – and the engraving of the newspaper flutters. The pages turn faster and faster, emitting a howling gale that bowls you head over foot. When you pick yourself up, you are inside a vast attic full of books and bricabrac, lit from one side by windows that offer no view of the outside world – just light and mist.

Tarnation! You have been lured into the eternal prison of Sunday Afternoon. Fortunately, there are several ways to escape. Each of the arcane objects before you is secretly a portal, transporting you to another site of arcane activity, in a bizarre web of diversions that cannot possibly reflect the hand of a human curator. Which will you choose?

As you step forward, your toe nudges an ornamental scroll. It growls and wriggles like a panicking caterpillar, scooting away under a table. Before you lose sight of it, you discern the title and subject of the text – it's an essay by Kyle Tam about the yokai of Promise Mascot Agency.

Deep in a drawer, you discover a sour-smelling binder full of extracts from an ancient and all but indecipherable dispute over the discovery of "generative AI" in something called "Big Walk". The stakes are long-buried, but many of the individual pieces of writing are lively. Here is Bruno Dias noting in passing that "one of the harms of the 'AI' political project is the propaganda machine dedicated to making you feel stupid and helpless." Here is a professorial interjection from Brendan Keogh calling on the warring parties to recognise when "critiques of generative AI are actually just deflected critiques of the capitalist relations of technology and labour". Here is Mike Cook arguing that "what's happening is not unusual, it's not extreme, it's not unfair and it's not a 'public flogging'." Here is a ticker tape message from Hannah Nicklin observing that "if your radical position doesn’t have room for transformation it will not be safe until it contains just you".

A footnote in the same dusty sheaf of papers points you towards another work from Mike Cook in a different drawer. This one consists of neon slides, slotted into an antique View-Master, and explores a comparison between procedural generation and street photography.

Peering at the weirdly white and opaque windowpanes, you realise there are intricate equations traced in the condensation. It appears to be a post-mortem for a "post-cosy" game called Danchi Days, in which developer Melos Han-Tani discusses wishlist conversion rates and the problem of not fitting neatly into any recognisable genre.

A snowglobe stands on a mantelpiece, the flakes still orbiting a miniature washtub as though the object had been recently shaken, even though the chamber has clearly been abandoned for decades. You put it to your ear, anticipating the faint jingle of Xmas bells. Instead, you are almost deafened by a screeching guitar chord. Here is Erin Keane to explain.

Next to the snowglobe on the mantelpiece, there's a souvenir shop conch shell, polished to a high sheen. You put that to your ear, hoping to catch the soothing shuffle of surf on shingle, and a disembodied voice tells you to piss off. Tim Sniffen has some thoughts about gentrification, and why only he should be allowed to do it.

Again, one of these mystic artefacts hides the key to your release from the suffocating stillness of Sunday Afternoon. Which will you choose? Or have you, perhaps, brought a sorcerous teleportation device of your own? Please share. Here is Joanna Newsom's Cosmia to help you think.

#3983. Why Do I Want To Paint The Walls In Grand Theft Auto VI?

I admire the cozy sim genre. Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing are on regular rotation in my home on my family’s screens, but not my own. In an odd way, I find the genre stressful, arguably the opposite of its intended purpose. I will happily and cathartically guide Grace Ashcroft through the tense hallways of Rhodes Hill in Resident Evil Requiem, but Pokémon Pokopia’s seemingly endless list of to-dos makes me sweat. It’s just not my genre, and I have come to terms with that.

Grand Theft Auto VI is not a cozy game, but it has a substantial amount of cozy elements and mechanics. Bird (and animal) watching, for example, is apparent and encouraged early in the experience. You can also fix up your somewhat dilapidated home from almost the moment you are let loose outside of the opening tutorial missions.

And for some reason, I couldn’t start that process fast enough.

I climbed to the roof to fix the leak and replaced all the stairs leading up to the home before I ever participated in the game’s namesake and stole a car. Normally, it’s the kind of interaction I skip or choose not to engage with, given the option. Or, I do the bare minimum to progress. Sure, I have all the options in the world to build and decorate a house and make it my own, but… that feels like a lot of work. And I am not an artist.

The “cozy” elements of Grand Theft Auto VI are admittedly different from those in a game like Pokopia or Animal Crossing. You’re not designing your home (though you can pick a paint color), but it feels similar, and I am trying to figure out why I enjoy it here as opposed to other games. Is it because Jason and Lucia are so instantly believable as human beings that I want their home to be nicer?

After some thought, I think it might just come down to Grand Theft Auto VI’s consistently impressive visual fidelity. Replacing the shingles on the roof, for example, offers a close-up look at Jason’s character model, and you can practically feel the texture of the asphalt while the heat of the sun beats down.

I don’t have confirmation, but it also just feels like someone at Rockstar did exhaustive research on what the process of replacing a roof shingle should look like, even if, I’m sure, it probably doesn’t quite work that way in the real world. Jason makes it look incredibly easy, to the point that it had me questioning if I should be climbing up to my own roof and taking care of some loose shingles myself. And you know what is a lot of fun? Watching someone who is good at something do the thing they’re good at.

I’m now into the driving and shooting part of the game (and enjoying that, too!), but I am shocked at how grateful I was to have the option to stay home and put up drywall.

#3982. You're not crazy, trying to heal in Nioh 3 sometimes doesn't work - and Team Ninja is fixing it

One of the more insidiously aggravating bugs in Nioh 3 makes it so the game ignores you when you try to use elixirs, but hopefully not for long.

Nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an issue that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an issue that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

Spoilers for the end of Mass Effect 3 follow, naturally.

You know what? I didn't have many questions left at the end of Mass Effect 3. Joker was a robot now. His robot girlfriend was perhaps less of a robot? Shepard converted herself into a dotfile to make the Reapers chill out, and Buzz Aldrin's talents lie in areas other than voice acting.

I had plenty of questions when BioWare announced Mass Effect 5 was gonna be a thing though. Could you really write a Mass Effect story in the radically changed galaxy we were left with at the end of Shepard's adventure? Apparently, you could. In a recent AMA on Reddit (via IGN), BioWare writer Cat Valente wrote that the now-cancelled Mass Effect sequel's team put a lot of work into handling ME3's endings "in a way that wouldn't piss everyone off, [or] at least not piss them off completely".

The goal, says Valente, was to write a continuation of Mass Effect's narrative that "wouldn't privilege any one kind of player over another". That tracks with what we've heard before: leaks have suggested ME5 was set to more or less wrap all the previous game's endings into one (Deus Ex: Invisible War style, hell yeah).

Of course, it'd have to do that while allowing BioWare "to actually write a coherent story going forward, within the limits of having to do it in a playable mainstream videogame and not a post-modern 3000 page novel", adds Valente. "Not for nothing, guys, but that's *kind of a tall fucking order*. Part of the reason it took so long and Andromeda was in Andromeda is that figuring out an elegant solution to that problem turns out to be *really hard*".

The sheer challenge of creating a coherent, satisfying follow-up to ME3 that took into account everyone's choices had Valente, at one point, "thinking *god, if I'd known when I finished ME3 that I'd be one of the people who had to find the mops and buckets to clean up that mess...*".

Nevertheless, she reckons the studio did eventually alight on a way of handling it that made sense. "Yes, there was an answer, yes, I know it, as least inasmuch as I know what it was when I was working there… We knew all the discourse on the endings, of course we did, and I do think as a fan I would have been happy with the solution (at least what it was when I left) if I booted up the game having had nothing to do with it".

#3980. Grand Theft Auto VI's Auto Drive Is A Beautiful And Free Version Of Hands-Free Travel

Grand Theft Auto VI is a game where you spend a lot of time behind the wheel. Always has been. But sometimes, you just won't feel like actively driving, but you also don't to waste money on a cab.

This is where Auto Drive comes in. It lets the game take over and drive you where you need to go in real time and all with a cinematic camera that shifts and moves, letting you take in the environment without all that pesky "having to pay attention to the road." Red Dead Redemption 2 had the same feature, and I have fond memories of taking advantage of it to watch Arthur ride his horse through that game's incredible environment. It's a great option in GTAVI, but how to use it and turn it on isn't immediately apparent.

First, you must select a destination. Get the GPS set up to direct you to where you want to go.

Next, start driving. The Auto Drive is smart, but doesn't seem to be smart enough to make three-point turns or back out of parking lots. You need to be on your way before you can turn it on.

Once you're on the path, hold down in the d-pad and press start to activate Cinematic.

Once you've done this you should be able to hold down the Circle button on PlayStation or the B button on Xbox to activate Auto Drive and... voilà! You can sit back and let Jason or Lucia take the wheel. They will drive legally, even stopping at lights, but you can speed them up if they're taking too long.

I've always enjoyed driving in Grand Theft Auto, but I was grateful to find this almost-hidden option early in the game.

#3979. "We've finally reached this milestone": Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP kicks off open beta after around six years preparing for cybermayhem

"Let's see how the project handles real player traffic"

After a couple of years of regular testing behind closed doors, Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta, giving anyone who fancies a bit of multi-merc action a chance to give it a go. Though, if you do, be prepared for bugs and crashes, as work on the mod is far from over with the release of this "true beta".

As shown off in the video above, CyberMP's not about being able to play through the base game's missions with friends, but rather cruise around Night City as a gang getting into races and PvP shootouts. In that regard, it seems more akin to GTA 4's online mode than GTA 5's, with classic improvised hijinks the main draw over being able to pull off gigs with a crew. Though, there do also look to be roleplaying servers which could scratch the itch of those more interested in pretending to be a merc than blowing up other people's rides.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders wrote on Discord. "Anyone can jump in and play now — no invites or applications needed. Fair warning: this is a true beta. Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers. We welcome everyone: regular players, future server admins, and those who just love breaking game mechanics."

"Right now, our absolute priority is stability and fixing crashes," they continued later in the post. "New features are planned, but we need to polish the foundation first. A huge thank you to everyone who has been with us since the early versions, helped with closed testing, and patiently waited. We've finally reached this milestone. Let's see how the project handles real player traffic!"

According to the modders, CyberMP's "client doesn't have a digital signature yet", which could cause antivirus software not to be a fan of it. They're also anticipating "problems with the anti‑cheat system", so it may be worth holding off on giving the mod a go if you're not keen on being trolled by someone with the sort of destructive power usually reserved for megacorps and AIs from beyond the blackwall in the Cyberpunkverse.

For info on how to get CyberMP up and running, as well as create a custom server dedicated to the likes of roleplay or races, head over to its website. As you might expect, the mod requires a legit copy of Cyberpunk bought on either Steam, GOG, or the Epic store.

#3978. Genshin Impact Luna 5 takes the squad back to Mondstadt, finally makes Varka playable

Genshin Impact's next update will have you reminiscing about the good ol' days of... 2020.

The latest big content update has been revealed for HoYoverse's breakout game, Genshin Impact. Version Luna 5, which has the unusually long and needlessly layered title — Song of the Welkin Moon: Variation - Homeward, He Who Caught the Wind — is set to arrive February 25.

This one is a bit of a nostalgia play, taking everyone back to Mondstadt, the place where you may remember taking your first steps. And, as with any good return to the ol’ hunting grounds, come familiar characters, too.

The big new arrival is Varka, who joins as a playable character for the first time. Varka, Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, is a character whose debut has been long-awaited. He is a 5-Star Anemo Claymore wielder with a dual-wield combat style, capable of dealing two different types of Elemental damage. His addition means that there's now finally a burly 5-Star male character of each elemental type... do with that information what you will.

Varka's dual-wielding combat style allows him to deal two different types of Elemental damage at the same time. The way it works is that his Elemental Skill boosts the damage of his regular attacks, but it also converts the damage type of his right-hand claymore to match his teammates’ elements (Pyro, Hydro, Electro, or Cryo). The left-hand claymore always deals Anemo damage.

The more normal attacks you use, the more frequently he can activate a special Elemental Skill, or trigger a Charged Attack that doesn’t consume stamina. He can also rely on the Hexerei effect to trigger more instances of Elemental Skill, as well as Charged Attacks, making him a monster damage-dealer.

Varka, of course, has been a staple member of the cast, featuring in both the original story in a small cameo, as well as taking a bigger role in the recent Nod-Krai chapters. With the return to Mondstadt, his playable debut makes sense. His Story Quest will shed light on his encounter with the Wild Hunt, and the Great Wolf King of the North

The reruns for this version are going to be Flins — who will be available in the first phase of Event Wishes — as well as Skirk and Escoffier in the second phase. You can also look forward to the return of the Chronicled Wish with Mondstadt characters.

Staying on the theme of reminiscence, the big event in Luna 5 is centered around revisiting memories from the beginning of your time with Genshin Impact, and reuniting with old friends. In Echoes of Memory, you’ll witness familiar scenes that have been changed slightly, and you’ll need to use the Spotter Kamera to detect and record those differences.

The Knights of Favonius are hosting several other activities for everyone to take part in, including an event that lets you catch up with old friends over drinks which you make for them.

Outside of events, there’s a new set of Gliding and Combat Challenges. And, of course, there are new minigames that you can relax with. The Kamera is being utilised yet again, and this time you can use to capture sights from your time in spots across Natlan, Fontaine, and Sumeru. There’s also… a horde mode of a sort, where you fend off waves of enemies.

#3977. "Nobody was hurt" in shooting near Clockwork Revolution devs InXile Entertainment's office, the Xbox-owned studio and police confirm

"Nobody was hurt" in a shooting last week near the California office of Clockwork Revolution developers InXile, both the studio and local police have confirmed. The incident, which took place on November 11th, is currently being investigated and police have reportedly taken a suspect into custody.

"Officers got there [on November 11th]," Tustin police sergeant Christopher Peterson said in statement to Aftermath. "They responded to a report of a drive-by shooting there. Located multiple shell casings. Nobody was hurt. Processed the crime scene, and then sometime [Friday] morning, a little before 11 [AM], they took a suspect into custody. And the investigation is still kind of ongoing as to where and why."

"We’re relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," a spokesperson for InXile said in a separate statement. "Our focus is on supporting our team, and we are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate."

InXile are set to release steampunk RPG Clockwork Revolution next year. The studio, developers of the likes of Wasteland 3 and The Bard's Tale IV, are one of the few Xbox-owned studios not to have been affected - at least as of writing - by Microsoft's ongoing mass layoffs this year.

Since being announced in 2023, Clockwork Revolution's dripped with Bioshock-ish vibes and popped up semi-regularly at Xbox showcases. "Wield the power of an incredible device to travel back in time, changing the past and rewriting the future of the city you call home: the vibrant steampunk metropolis of Avalon," reads its Steam synopsis. "In this immersive RPG, you'll step into the shoes of Morgan Vanette, a fully customizable player-character and member of the Rotten Row Hooligans. Travel between past and present as you battle the ruthless Lady Ironwood, who has been manipulating time to keep the working class struggling while amassing immense wealth and power."

Best wishes to the staff at InXile, here's hoping that going forwards they're able to get with making what's looking to be an intriguingly funky game without enduring any more concerning incidents like this one.

GTA 6 is the first game in the series to make me feel bad, like really bad, for yeeting innocent cyclists into the Gulf of Leonida with the velocity of a pickup truck at 120 miles per hour. It doesn't stop me from doing it, but every time I find myself covering my mouth with my hand in horror and loading up a previous save, preserving the innocence of a Jason or Lucia without the human-shaped blood splatter on their truck hood. Empathy is another word for the feeling I have toward Leonidans, and it's very much by design.

Rockstar intentionally designed GTA 6 with a built-in criminal profile system that discourages what in-game warnings describe as "psycho" behavior, which is also a permanent label you can acquire if you act like I do consistently without save-scumming. This evolution from Red Dead Redemption 2's honor system is a first for the GTA series and a minor point of contention amid unanimous praise for the game, but Rockstar co-founder Rob Nelson tells Eurogamer that it's simply more fun to play the game as if the NPCs whizzing around the world are actual people. It certainly helps that they look pretty darn close to real humans this time around.

"I think as the resolution goes up, it sort of asks different new questions," says Nelson. "As the resolution goes up, you want the sophistication of the experience to go up, and obviously the sophistication of the mechanics. So it just naturally flowed that we give players choices to interact with the world beyond just violence, beyond just 'down the barrel of a gun', because it's fun ... It's fun for some people like myself to just sort of role-play in the world, and be in the world, and restraint becomes something you hadn't thought about."

Empathy is a bit of a contradiction to the old GTA fantasy of rampaging indiscriminately through a city helpless to your whimsy, but Nelson is right that there's so much more depth to GTA 6 that makes that sort of stuff feel one-dimensional by comparison. Even compared to GTA 5, I find myself exponentially more immersed cruising around Leonidas, and a lot of that comes down to how lifelike its inhabitants are.

"If you think about the NPCs, even back to [GTA] 5, you would draw a weapon - first of all, they didn't react if you drew an invisible shotgun out of nowhere, or a rocket launcher," Nelson says. "They don't react unless you aim it, and then they flee in terror, and you're just sort of this demigod stomping through the world, you know? And that's fun, but for how long?"

If the answer to that question for you is, 'endlessly', you can still choose that life in GTA 6, but you'll eventually reach an irreversible stage in your criminal profile that will permanently alter the way NPCs react and interact with you. "You choose. You're trying to jack somebody off a motorcycle, and they pull a gun on you, and you have to blow their head off and it's like, 'You shouldn't have made me do that!'" Nelson says.

"And so then it has more meaning, and it's more funny in a way when it's a little bit more pointed. And you can still go on those rampages and basically smash your Criminal Profile until it breaks and then you enter this irredeemable state, which basically says 'I reject your criminal profile system! I don't want it.'"

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

It's a testament to GTA 6's strong writing that I care far too much about Jason and Lucia's relationship to let either of them reach that point in the game's honor system. I'll probably never resist the urge to hijack a nice car in a GTA game, but in this latest iteration, I'll pretty much always load up an old save afterward and role-play as a petty criminal at worst.

#3974. Nioh 3 is, unsurprisingly, the fastest-selling game in the series with over a million units sold

Nioh 3 has taken the Nioh franchise to new heights, delivering its biggest-ever launch.

Even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Today, publisher Koei Tecmo has announced that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

On Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

Nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”

If you’re curious about the challenging and very rewarding action RPG, start with these gameplay tips, and don’t be shy to call upon a friend (or stranger) for help using our co-op guide.

It's a temporary congestion measure, but it might be around to stay.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"To help alleviate server congestion following the release of Patch 8.0, we will be enabling cross-region Data Center Travel between the North American and European data centers during scheduled maintenance on Tuesday, December 1, 2026.

"… We will continue to take community feedback into account as we carefully evaluate the possibility of permanently enabling travel between the North American and European data centers, as well as opening travel between other physical data centers," via the Lodestone.

I play Final Fantasy 14 on the US servers—which is a problem, because I live in the UK. I do so because, well, some of my closest friends are on those servers, too; but also because there's a slightly livelier roleplay community bustling on the US side of things, and I'm a roleplayer who likes squeezing my warrior of light like he's a stress toy.

As a result, I've often stared longingly at the people who play in the UK due to the crime of my time zone: Unable to play with my UK friends, unable to join a static raiding group that starts at a reasonable hour, and unable to play the game without terrible animation lock on my abilities. Unless I, say, broke ToS and used an addon that brought me on-par with people who have 30 ping, hypothetically. Which I don't do.

Square Enix has thrown open these doors, however, to mainly deal with congestion troubles:

"As peak play times differ between North America and Europe, another physical data center may be less crowded and serve as a viable option when login queues on your usual data center are long. While players connecting from geographically distant locations may experience increased latency, we encourage you to try playing on a different physical data center before the expansion launches."

However, they know that people like me have expressed their yearning to hop between the good ol' USA and Europe: "However, we have received ongoing feedback from players wishing to travel between the North American and European data centers, and many players in both regions are able to communicate in English even when it is not their first language."

All in all, this'll be a huge quality of life improvement. There might be some difficulties, though: raiding culture can vary drastically even between logical datacenters like Aether and Crystal, let alone between continents. However, I'd be shocked if the differences between US and EU raiding cultures were insurmountable; JP and US? Might be a bigger deal.
