Hacker was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

Kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the company contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent company Take-Two quickly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

Hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely shows anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

#3969. Intel are being sued for "misleading" investors about "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory" thanks to AI-fuelled price hikes

Tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they announced a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

The lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year.

The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen".

They also accuse the company of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above."

Finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Company chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales."

Once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. As regards graphics cards, they have long been dwarfed by Nvidia.

Any Intel investor who wants a piece of that lawsuit has until January 12th 2027 to sign up as a lead plaintiff – that is, a court appointee who represents the interests of other class members. As regards us little people who don't buy stock in huge technology corporations, all this merely continues the weird existential crisis wrought upon 'traditional' gaming and computing hardware by the feckless quest to sell a better chatbot.

#3968. The Video Games You Should Play This Weekend – November 20, 2026

This is it. We finally made it. Grand Theft Auto VI is here. I have played the game for a number of hours and read Matt Miller's glowing review, which you can read here, and I still don't know if I personally believe the game is actually out. But that just might the lack of sleep from staying up late to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

Many games chose to avoid the blast radius of Rockstar's latest crime caper, but that doesn't mean it's the only game that came out this week and you can find them below. But as is tradition, here are some of our top stories of the week first.

If you’re not aware that GTAVI launched this week, it’s possible that you’ve been living under a rock somewhere. Nonetheless, we’re here to offer the reminder that after more than a decade of waiting for a new installment, Rockstar has this week rolled out its new game. It’s good. Like, really good, and if you’re an adult who plays video games, it should really be a title you make time for.

In my review, I highlighted some of its many positive traits, but as you prepare to dive into its criminal delights over the weekend, one element I’d especially like to point out is its viability as a game to play with your partner. Like an excellent prestige TV crime show, GTAVI is a game that features a rich, dramatic, funny, and well-written story that I genuinely believe has the potential to be a good time for both a player and a viewer, though, admittedly, the person who gets to enjoy running the sticks is probably having the most fun.

However you plan to enjoy it, here’s hoping Grand Theft Auto VI turns out to be worth the wait you’ve likely had for it. For my part, it certainly has been, and I suspect you’ll find it only gets better the deeper into the game you go.

The running joke publisher Devolver Digital has made with this “spectacular remaster of the original remake of the unreleased action-platformer starring the most famous video game mascot of all time” is that it launched the same day as Grand Theft Auto VI. Volvy’s Adventure has been positioned as a tongue-in-cheek competitor to Rockstar’s behemoth, with Devovler even releasing a trailer that is a shot-for-shot parody of GTA VI’s. While I’ve chuckled at these stunts, Volvy’s Adventure isn’t just a joke game. It’s actually pretty fun.

For one, it’s developed by a respectable studio in Doinksoft, the team behind fun indie games like Gato Roboto, Gunbrella, and this year’s Dark Scrolls. Vovly’s Adventure is a 16-bit 2D platformer where players use Volvy’s oversized fist to punch through objects, which, in turn, propels him in the same direction. Thus, platforming is a fast-paced and explosive exercise in soaring fist-first through barriers and enemies, collecting items, and burrowing through certain platforms. The platforming feels pretty good, and it’s backed by a catchy soundtrack; the destruction is satisfying; and the levels are relatively brief, making it easy to plow through.

I wasn’t sure what to expect from Volvy’s Adventure beyond the marketing jokes, but it’s got some sauce. Sitting at the budget price of $5 (and a launch discount of $3.74), it’s a curiosity that’s easy to check out.

Australia Did It, from Rami Ismail and his team at Aesthetician Labs, hit a little snag with its publicized release date. Valve got backed up approving the release of games on its platform and a handful of games were affected. Australia Did It, despite the unexpected delay, is out... and it's good! Here's what Brian Shea wrote in his review: "Looking back on the hours I poured into Australia Did It, the forgettable train segments will occupy only a small part of my memories, just as they do in each run. Instead, what will stick with me for months to come are the creative combination mechanics, the outstanding turn-based defense system, and the thrill of uncovering the mysteries of this bleak, yet engaging world."

God of War Sons of Sparta is... underwhelming, to be blunt. You can read my review here. The game is a prequel where you play as a young Kratos and go on a 2D Metroid-inspired adventure with your brother, Deimos. If you are interested in getting the full God of War story, there are some interesting narrative and character details in the game, but it has some shortcomings. What's surprising about its re-release this week is that it is now available on PS4. An unexpected "new" platform to say the least.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The premature death of BioWare is made even sadder by the fact that many of its best games were never remastered or remade for modern hardware, and now they probably never will be. Compare that to an RPG studio like Bethesda, which is notorious for endlessly remastering, re-releasing, and porting The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim, and it's easy to see why BioWare diehards feel like they were dealt a bad hand by the studio's parent company, EA.

Not to rub salt into the wound, but former Dragon Age lead Mark Darrah, a BioWare veteran who worked at the studio for more than two decades, Dragon Age: Origins could've easily been remastered and probably would've sold pretty well if it weren't for EA's reluctance to remake or remaster anything.

Talking to Pembridge TV (timestamp), Darrah says a big reason EA doesn't typically modernize its older games is because a big portion of its IP catalog is annual sports games like EA Sports FC and NHL. "What are you gonna take NHL 2005 and do a 20th anniversary remaster? What? You have an NHL. NHL never went away. Madden never went away. Football Club never went away," Darrah says.

That doesn't explain why series like Mass Effect and Dragon Age didn't get more remasters (on that, Darrah simply says "they don't get it"), but Darrah says the opportunity was there even if Skyrim levels of ports wouldn't work.

"Honestly, yeah, I don't know that anyone other than Bethesda could get away with porting Skyrim to every single platform and selling a million copies every single time they do that," he says, adding, "But yes! We could have remastered Origins probably twice and sold a couple million copies each time."

#3966. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#3965. Grand Theft Auto VI Shatters Records, Making $3.79 Billion In 24 Hours As The Biggest Entertainment Launch Ever

Grand Theft Auto VI dropped yesterday to massive success, and while we expected it to do well, hearing the numbers behind the historic launch day is still staggering. According to a statement obtained by Bloomberg's Jason Schreier and IGN, Rockstar has confirmed that the open-world juggernaut made $3.79 billion in 24 hours. This makes it not just the biggest video game launch of all time – it's the biggest entertainment launch of all time, and it's not especially close.

Schreier goes on to confirm that much of that money comes from GTA VI's record-breaking pre-orders. It turns out, there were 32.5 million pre-sales, which is a truly mind-bending number. For context, its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, currently the second best-selling game of all time, sold 11.21 million copies in the first 24 hours – GTAVI nearly triples that figure. In pre-orders alone, the game has become the 30th best-selling game of all time, with more copies sold in the first day than Elden Ring and Super Mario Odyssey have sold, period.

In terms of the dollar amount, GTAVI's $3.79 billion in 24 hours is not just more money than any film has made in its opening weekend; it's more money than any movie has ever made in the box office – even Avengers: Endgame, which currently holds the highest worldwide gross, is still shy of $3 billion after several successful theatrical runs.

Grand Theft Auto VI also set the record on Metacritic for the highest-reviewed game of all time (with an average critic score of 99), and it headlined this week's rollout of the Game Awards 2026 nominees, with more nominations than any other game. We also loved it, and our editor-in-chief Matt Miller scored it a perfect 10.

#3964. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

I cannot get over all the ways Rockstar has turned a controller into an immersion tool.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I hate to credit Sony's aggressive (and presumably very expensive) marketing campaign for GTA 6—you know, the one which appeared to have also plucked the ability for Xbox to even mention the game by name. That's something I'm still shocked was even a thing anyone was allowed to do.

So I won't credit it… mostly. We all already know that PC is going to get the best version of GTA 6 when it finally hits our desktops, whenever that might be. But I am going to agree with one part of the whole "Grand Theft Auto 6 plays best on PS5" shtick: the DualSense controller. It's so good that I fear those who reach for a mouse and keyboard will be missing out on some incredible immersion.

I never expected a controller to actively add to my experience, but I also forgot just how many goodies Sony stuffed into this thing. Seriously, Rockstar has taken full advantage of everything the peripheral has to offer.

I've been weaving through traffic way more in GTA 6 thanks to a huge increase in general vehicle density and some criminally narrow roads that can cause some major bottlenecks. Flooring it all the way from A to B isn't quite as easy as it used to be, which is why I kind of love how you can use the adaptive triggers to comfortably maintain a steady cruising speed before clicking it all the way in as a way to floor it. It makes my speed feel just that little more deliberate, with that tactile feel for when I really want to amp up how fast I'm going.

But driving might actually be the least interesting way Rockstar has made full use of the controller. The parts that have gotten me more than anything are the small ways haptics have been implemented to strengthen story moments or make parts of Leonida feel even more alive.

The first time I really noticed the controller was back in the beginning of the game, when I'm instructed to go and pick Lucia up from prison. As I'm standing outside as Jason, watching her emerge from the gate, the controller starts thumping just a little bit. A heartbeat. I'm literally feeling Jason's heart racing as Lucia approaches. No dialogue, no internal monologue letting me know how nervous he is. It's such a small detail, but one that massively hammed up the moment for me.

My absolute favourite way it's been implemented, though? The clubs. The goddamn clubs. Leonida's sprawling nightlife is already impressive in isolation—Hitman's Berlin level was the last time I felt this enamoured with a videogame nightclub—but this is where Rockstar went all-in on the controller's haptic feedback. Step into a club and you'll immediately feel the bass pulsating through the controller.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It's not just the same, monorhythmic beat for every song though. The bass perfectly matches the song; those long, teeth-shaking booms cut with shorter, less intense thumps. I feel like I'm back in my first year of university trying to sleep while the nearby student nightclub blasts the same songs until 3am every damn Wednesday, the bass somehow reverberating across the campus and straight through my bedframe.

When I first set foot inside the Jack of Hearts club at the beginning of Chapter 3, I was practically stunlocked by how much more immersive being able to feel the bass through the controller was making the entire experience. Seriously, I cannot overstate just how much it sucks you into what's happening around you.

These are all things that I genuinely feel folks are going to miss out on with a simple mouse and keyboard. Sure, your aiming will be better. Yes, none of the things I've described above actually change anything about the gameplay. It'll still be the same GTA 6 no matter what you play with. But for all the ways Rockstar has managed to elevate the experience and the immersion I've been feeling just through something as small as the controller I'm holding? It at least deserves consideration for your go-to playthrough peripheral.

#3961. Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be announced, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a new GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

The influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

The city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

Much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

The Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on New Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. But I'm even more pleased that as the studio's aged, their work has grown closer to Illusion Softworks'.

Sam Corcos is vibe-coding Legatum, a "historical 4X on a hex map, built for people who love Civilization"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While DOGE itself is long dead, some of the officials appointed by the Elon Musk-backed organization remain part of the United States government. That includes Sam Corcos, who joined the Treasury Department as special advisor in 2025 and soon became chief information officer there. Corcos remains in that position amid a heavily scrutinized cybersecurity breach at the department, but that hasn't stopped him from finding the time to continue vibe-coding his Civilization clone.

Yes, Corcos is creating a game, in the loosest terms, called Legatum, which is a "historical 4X on a hex map, built for people who love Civilization." Taking specific inspiration from Civilization 6, it's "familiar on purpose," according to the GitHub readme, letting you choose a civilization and build alliances or make war on rivals as progress through nine eras and try to build the greatest empire of all.

"Legatum is built largely with AI coding agents, and all of its art is AI-generated," that readme explains. "Most of the art comes from OpenAI's image models through ChatGPT; the icons and heraldry are SVG drawn by scripts in this repository. The working files are public so that other people can learn from them."

Dozens upon dozens of updates have been made to Legatum in the past few days, a fact that has drawn some scrutiny given that the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, a bureau of the Treasury Department, is in the midst of dealing with a self-described "cybersecurity incident."

A notice on FinCEN's website notes that the breach has "resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline." While few details on this incident have been made public, a breach of a US bureau dedicated to fighting financial crime does seem like an 'all hands on deck' situation that would give the organization's CIO something more important to do.

For his part, Corcos tweets that "the computers are doing it on their own. Mostly Opus 5.5 orchestrating a bunch of iterative loops." But, as 404 Media notes, he's finding time to regularly give feedback to Claude on new features and tweaks that should be made for Legatum.

Using GitHub's issue tracker, users have noted a problem with the code: "Treasury CIO is too busy vibecoding instead of doing his job." Several comments seem to agree, but Corcos eventually closed the discussion as "off-topic," since the "tracker is for bugs and ideas about the Legatum game." This response was also generated by Claude.

#3959. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#3958. Deborah Ann Woll Will Reprise Her Role As Laufey In Amazon's God Of War Series

Deborah Ann Woll, likely best known as Karen Page in Daredevil and Daredevil: Born Again, has just been cast as Laufey in the upcoming live-action God of War series. It's a perfect fit, not just because she's a great actress – Woll already portrays the character in the video games.

The live-action God of War series is currently in production, and after a series of headlines about Kratos, it's refreshing to get some news about his late wife, Faye. Also known as Laufey, she dies right before 2018's God of War (which the show is based on) begins. The game centers on a journey between Kratos and his son to spread Faye's ashes from the highest peak in the realms.

Faye is not present in 2018's God of War, but she appears in God of War Ragnarök in flashback and dream sequences. In this game, she's played by Deborah Ann Woll, an oddly high-profile casting for a relatively minor character. It all made sense earlier this year, however, when we learned Woll will reprise her role as the star of God of War Laufey, which tells Faye's story as she fights through a mythological underworld.

It's a cool piece of news, and it implies that Faye will have more of a presence in the series than in the first game, where she never appears at all. As for what shape that presence takes, we have no idea.

Woll joins the likes of Alastair Duncan, who plays Mimir and will also reprise his role. The two don't really interact in the games, however, so it's unlikely to see them share the screen in the series.

The main news around Prime Video's God of War is about its protagonist. Originally announced as Ryan Hurst, the actor suffered a serious injury on the set of the show and was replaced by Dave Bautista (Guardians of the Galaxy, Glass Onion) in August. Other key cast members include Callum Vinson as Atreus, Sonya Walger as Freya, Mandy Patinkin as Odin, and Ed Skrein as Baldur.

For more God of War, you can look forward to Woll's portrayal of Faye in God of War Laufey, though it recently got delayed.

#3957. My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

Longing for the Venetian Dogehouse, stuck in the Venetian doghouse

The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching new lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

This is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

Getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

If you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

When you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your company can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

If you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a new branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

In the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

As the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

Thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for said Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

Not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the big chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

What I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing new folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

Much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

Thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a new piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

While I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

#3956. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#3955. One Of Our Favorite Action Games From Gamescom, Showa American Story, Has Been Delayed To 2027

Showa American Story is set in a world where Japan's 1980s economic prowess was strong enough to purchase America, and so it did. Taking place in Neo Yokohama, formerly Hollywood, this raunchy, zany action game was one of our favorites at Gamescom 2026, but unfortunately, we'll have to wait a little longer than expected to experience more of this adventure.

That's because developer Nekcom Entertainment and publisher 4Divinity have revealed that Showa American Story has been delayed to next year. Originally due out sometime this year (though it became clear that wasn't going to happen given the radio silence as we near the year's end), Showa American Story will now launch on PlayStation 5 and PC on October 28, 2027.

"Reaching this milestone after five years of development means a lot to our entire team," the studio writes in a statement. "With core game content now complete, we're dedicating our full focus to polishing and optimizing the experience so that when you step into Showa American Story, it feels cohesive, responsive, and complete. Thank you for your continued support, enthusiasm, and patience along the way. We can't wait to welcome you on October 28, 2027."

In the meantime, read Game Informer's Showa American Story hands-on preview from this year's Gamescom. After that, check out our list of the top 10 action games to play right now.

#3954. Spirit Crossing, the new Zelda-ish hangout MMO from the creators of Cozy Grove, understands that sometimes you just want to be alone

New multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

Spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

You can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

As has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

It's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

The true box office winner of Dunesday has been predicted by the Nielsen ratings, and it's none other than Avengers: Doomsday.

Per Deadline, NRG (National Research Group, owned by Nielsen) predicts that Doomsday will bring in $270 million at the global box office during its opening weekend. Dune 3 is predicted to bring in $75 million.

This is the highest projection NRG has ever recorded, with Spider-Man: Brand New Day being the second-highest. To date, Avengers: Endgame now holds the record second-highest opening weekend for any movie ever at $357.1M, having been beat out by Spider-Man: Brand New Day's $360 million.

Avengers: Doomsday tickets went on sale back in July for the special Infinity Vision screenings. Wanda will indeed return in Doomsday, but she won't be, uh, herself... if you catch my drift.

Dune 3 tickets have been a bit of a nightmare for fans as they sold out almost immediately back in April, and then crashed several movie theater apps when more tickets were released back in August. Oh, and, when tickets did sell out in April... people started reselling them for up to $1000. The people yearn for sand.

#3951. Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

How an unconventional peripheral became an equally unexpected survivor

PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a new physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming."

For Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

On release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

However, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

The answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Users were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device."

In the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for users. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

"I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he says. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find new uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat."

When looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal users: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the issue of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

All the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got big as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

Alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering users.

"I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day."

#3950. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

Taking Out Kitty Litter's lab locations in GTA 6 is a mission in Tyrone's questline, and sees you searching the city for 18 secret labs (after the first one he directs you to). Every lab has a red smoking chimney and a blue and white Spin On This laundry van parked outside.

It'll take a little while, but it's well worth it to get the unique gold SMG at the end. Plus, Tyrone will start buying narcotics from you for the highest price possible. To destroy each lab, simply shoot a smoking pink flask and then run away. I've also laid these out in the most optimal order, separated into regions, so you're not driving back and forth across Vice City.

Last note: if you want to unlock map markers for the labs yourself versus relying on these videos, you can threaten cooks in certain labs to potentially reveal them, or talk to Tyrone when you're fencing goods.

After you complete some missions for Tyrone (when you meet him with Dre'Quan during Dealer's Choice) he'll direct you to this trailer park in La Perle where you destroy the first Kitty Litter lab and start the hunt for the others. You can see the route to the lab in the video above.

You can find this one in the trailer park opposite Zenon's Pawn Shop Ammu-Nation in La Perle. As soon as you go through the main gate, you can see the trailer with the funnel chimney where they're cooking straight ahead. Sneak around the back and break inside to find the lab. Or take out the three guys in front and go in that way.

Just across the road from the Mezzasega Espresso and Slinger in the Decor District. Pull off to the right of the road into the Williams + Whitaker Homeware and Decor car park. You'll see a garage with a shutter at the far end with a smoking chimney and the laundry van parked. Open the shutter to find a lone guy in the lab.

This one is behind Peterson's Autoshop in Rockridge, directly south across the road from the Blessed Food Market, under the overpass, on the border between Rockridge and La Perle. Head through the main yard and turn left to spot the laundry van. Break into it, move it forward, and open the shutter behind to find the lab.

Just east of Fleeca Field stadium, next door to Xero Gas - Rockridge. You'll spot the blue and white laundry van parked off to the side of the road behind a wall. Head down that alley and turn right to find a garage door you can open with the lab inside.

On the east side of the condominium building directly south of the Vice City Hospital, by Emilio's Auto Center Gas. Look for the closed road with the laundry van parked at the southern end and some staircases and flats off to the side with the chimney spewing smoke. The lab is through the white door on the bottom floor.

Just down the road to the west of Bump and Grind coffee and Salon Belle, in a block of flats southeast of Fleeca Fields stadium. You can see the laundry van parked outside. The lab is on the upper floor on the left side in apartment 5, where you can see the smoking chimney. Break in via the front door to find the lab.

This lab is an easy one to find, around the back of Cross My Heart Tattoos. Head around the right side, turn left, and look to your left for the garage door with the guy sitting down guarding it, with the lab inside.

This lab is in the block of flats to the southeast of the Jack of Hearts and Urban Legendz, with the laundry van parked out front. Look inside apartment 103 on the first floor on the left side. It's quite hard to get away from this lab blowing up, so shoot it from outside and run away. Also this will likely cause a big shootout in the block, so book it.

This lab is to the southwest of your apartment in Chapter 3 and to the east of the Crosstown Mule - City Line marker. Look for an overgrown lot with the laundry van parked in it. The garage with the lab is just behind that.

This lab is directly west of Down Town Pawn, just between Rideout Customs and the Vargo's Gas station. Just past the gas station, look to the left where its fuel sign is to spot a laundry van, and further down the track, the garage with the lab and smoking chimney above it.

This lab is close to Xero Gas - Tequesta and west of Vice Seven Condominiums gym. When driving east to west past the station, turn right and keep an eye on your right towards the two floored condominiums for the laundry van parked outside. You want the set of staircases to the right of the van. Take the right side one up to the first floor to find the lab door directly ahead.

This lab is in a trailer park directly east down the road from Arrow Gas - VCIA, also west under the bridge from Pawn City and Vice City Firearms. Turn into the trailer park, take the first right and drive a little way around the corner to spot the trailer with the smoking chimney on the left. You can enter via a window around the other side to find the lab.

This lab is located in the far south of Salton, north of the Pay 'N' Spray - Salton, next door to the Slator Towing Inc robbery. Go around the south side of the derelict block of flats and climb the dumpster to jump up through the open window to find the lab.

This lab is west down the road from Xero Gas - Salton. Cross the train tracks, then keep an eye on your right for a carpark with a blue and white laundry van, then turn right into it to spot the building with the smoking chimney on the right. Hop the fence straight ahead and turn right to find one guy guarding the garage with the lab.

This lab is easy to find, directly south of Salon Perez and Safia Restaurant in Little Cuba. Look for some bungalows on the left with the laundry van parked outside. It's in the building with the chimney to the left of the one the van is parked in front of. The lab is the second door along.

This lab is north up the road from the Pay 'N' Spray - Balsero. Turn left down the alley with the laundry van parked to find a guy guarding the gate, a couple of guys inside, and the lab in an open garage further back behind them.

This lab is in a trailer park southeast from the Balasero jewelry stores, across the river. If driving from the east and the city, turn left before the bridge, turn right, then turn left and head a little way down to spot the trailer with the funnel chimney and laundry van outside. Sneak around back to get in and find the lab.

This lab is south across the river from Ron's Car Wash and Gas. Head over the bridge, across the junction, then keep an eye out to your left to spot where the laundry van is parked. The lab is just in the building beyond the gate with the smoking chimney. The door requires a code which is 1999 (referencing the billboard up to the right).

There are three main advantages to destroying all the Kitty Litter labs and completing the Spin On This mission with Tyrone and those are:

You'll also get $2,000 a lab, plus $10,000 for the Spin On This mission, meaning $48,000 altogether. Since I did everything, it's unclear to me whether these rewards are for destroying every lab, or the mission specifically that you get after you destroy 15 of them. Either way, if you want all of this, destroy all the labs in the city and complete the mission.

#3948. Grand Theft Auto VI Reaches Highest Concurrent Player Count Ever For PS5, More than 683 Million Hours Logged Already

Grand Theft Auto VI hasn't even been out for a week, and it's already broken so many records that it's hard to keep up. It made $3.79 billion in just 24 hours after its November 19 launch, making it the biggest entertainment launch of all time. It comes as no surprise, then, that Rockstar Games' latest crime saga is also shattering records specifically on PlayStation 5.

In a new PlayStation Blog post, the company has revealed that more than 39 million unique players have booted up GTA VI on PS5, with the game setting a new record for the highest number of concurrent players for any game on PlayStation, surpassing previous records across multiplayer games such as Helldivers II, free-to-play games like Fortnite, and single-player releases like Elden Ring. What's more, PS5 players have already logged a cumulative 683 million hours of GTA VI gameplay – that's nearly 78,000 years' worth of time.

Other records for GTA VI on PS5 include the game giving PlayStation the "largest number of newly connected PS5 consoles on a single day since the console's launch, outside of end-of-year holidays," and GTA VI being the first game played on 70% of new PS5 consoles since the game's launch.

This is likely only the beginning of records GTA VI will continue to break.

#3947. Judge denies motion to dismiss lawsuit accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of worsening RAM crisis by fixing memory prices and supply

Cue discussion of which activities hawks ordinarily do or don't do, as you'd expect

A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

The class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

The trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a new motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

"But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do."

You know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which currently looks likely to last until at least 2028.
