The Warlock’s initial unveiling, however, was incredibly brief, showing no gameplay. It also didn't explain how the class is going to fit within the existing roster. This all changes today.

Blizzard is bringing back its Developer Update livestream programme, which is the more structured, information-dense series of developer showcases. The focus of this one, of course, is going to mainly be on the Warlock class.

The Warlock is one of two classes coming to Diablo 4 with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion. The first, the Paladin, is already available in the game for anyone who pre-orders the expansion. The Warlock will instead arrive alongside the expansion on April 28.

The Developer Update will also include a first look at the game’s next season (Season 12), currently set for March 10. This mini season will only last until the expansion’s release, so it’s going to be interesting to see what it brings to the game.

You’ll be able to watch the showcase live at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, Twitch, and Twitter channels. We’ve embedded the YouTube and Twitch players below for your convenience.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.

#3945. Nioh 3 Comes To Xbox In January, Second Story DLC Launches Next Month

The Nioh series celebrates its 10th anniversary next February, and developer Team Ninja is celebrating with a pair of announcements for its latest entry, Nioh 3. First, the game's second story expansion, Bloody Insurrection, launches next month. Second, the game is coming to Xbox in January, marking the franchise's debut on Microsoft's platform.

Bloody Insurrection is Nioh 3's next story expansion following Hell Rising, which launched in August, and is set to release on December 18. Set in Shimabara in 1638, players will be at the center of a conflict between rebel forces, alchemists, and yokai while encountering familiar faces from previous Nioh games. Returning characters include Tachibana Muneshige from the original Nioh, and Bloody Insurrection will serve as the conclusion of protagonist Takechiyo's story.

Bloody Insurrection also introduces new Martial Arts for each weapon type, new Transformed Arts, Ninjutsu, Onmyo Magic, and Summoning Seals, and a new difficulty mode called Nioh's Journey. This new difficulty option is only available if you've completed the Enlightened One's Journey third playthrough and will allow players to find Ethereal equipment drops that let them acquire the highest rarity items in the game.

Additionally, Bloody Insurrection adds new endgame content called the Battlefield of Carnage. This challenges players with climbing floors, i.e., battlefields, filled with enemies and a boss. Each floor is divided into multiple battlefields, and defeating the floor's boss grants helpful battlefield effects, which can be combined to create unique synergies as you climb higher. Defeating enemies also lets players enhance special equipment "instilled with traces of the Yokai Realm," according to Koei Tecmo, which can only be found in Battlefield of Carnage.

A new edition of the game called Nioh 3: Complete Edition arrives on January 28 and will include the base game and its two story expansions. Complete Edition will arrive on PlayStation 5, PC, and, for the first time, Xbox Series X/S. The base version of Nioh 3 is also coming to Xbox Series X/S on the same date. The original version of Nioh 3 is also on sale at a 50 percent discount on PlayStation and Steam, and the season pass is 25 percent off.

For more on Nioh 3, be sure to read our review, in which we awarded the game a 9 out of 10. You can also check out our interview with Team Ninja discussing the Hell Rising expansion.

Ken Kutaragi says the Microsoft boss he met "was so arrogant"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ken Kutaragi led the development of Sony's video game consoles for years, and is widely known as "the father of the PlayStation." As it turns out, he might also be the father of the Xbox – or, at least, its distant uncle. In a new interview, Kutaragi claims to have been playing 4D chess in a meeting with a Microsoft executive, essentially tricking the company into creating its own game console.

"I had the chance to meet with the head of Microsoft one-to-one," Kutaragi tells The Game Business. The literal head of Microsoft in this era would, of course, have been Bill Gates, though Kutaragi isn't specific about who specifically he spoke to. Whoever it was, he wasn't terribly impressed: "He was so arrogant."

"Sony has no money, but they have huge money," Kutaragi continues. He showed this Microsoft executive what Sony was developing, and got an offer in return, where Microsoft would send "free hard disk drives to Sony" if they would, in exchange, "give some license rights" to Microsoft. "He tried to convince me," Kutaragi claims.

"I said only one word: 'No,'" he says. "'No thanks.' I was not so super arrogant as they were. I had a dream. If I say 'no,' they will get started on bringing in another platform after PC. That was my secret intention. They did, spending huge money on it."

The exact timeline here is unclear – Kutaragi doesn't specify whether it was the PS1 or the PS2 that he was quietly showing to Microsoft. Either way, by 2001, Microsoft had launched its own game console, the Xbox, as a direct competitor to PS2. Notably, one of the Xbox's key differentiators was its built-in hard drive, which may have been on the table for PS2 if Kutaragi hadn't shut Microsoft's offer down. Not that Sony had much reason to worry, since PS2 still outsold Xbox by several orders of magnitude.

Still, the rivalry between PlayStation and Xbox would drive the console market forward for many years to follow. "We, together, opened up this field," Kutaragi says. "That was very intentional."

#3943. Star Wars Galactic Racer will get local split-screen multiplayer in early 2027 with new 'Free Play' mode, finally letting racers yell at one another in a tangible space

Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an issue for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming update, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

It's come to my attention that some of us aren't having a very fun time with the NPCs in Grand Theft Auto 6. I've seen videos and threads of players complaining about not being able to steal cars because of crack head drivers, getting hunted down by killer NPCs, and just generally having a harder time traversing Leonida because who knows what bloodthirsty beast hides behind each corner? And to this I say, your steak is too buttery? Your lobster too juicy?

My first interaction with one of the unfriendly residents of Leonida started when I accidentally bumped into their car. Because I am wholly unaware of my surroundings, I didn't even notice that anyone was mad at me as I listened to my pop songs and carried on driving towards my mission. Little did I know that right behind me was a four-wheeler with a driver who had steam coming out of her ears.

So I pull up to the side of the road, ready to head in and start my mission, when seemingly out of nowhere the four-wheeler comes barreling in, almost taking me out completely. The driver gets out and starts screaming about payback. I have no idea what I've done, but this is GTA 6, I'm not taking this slander. So I start swinging.

The fight ends with me knocking this lady out, but she doesn't go down without a fight. At one point, I actually thought that was it for me—taken out on the pavement by a soccer mum, what a way to go.

But even if I had taken a long sleep on the sidewalk, that would've been OK, because it's all part of the beautiful package that GTA 6 offers.

I don't want vapid NPCs that buckle at the first sight of a handgun, or have the object permanence of a goldfish. Filling Leonida with some actually competent, and dare I say dangerous NPCs makes this game infinitely more interesting. I like not knowing how one small action will ruin my whole day, or having to be a little wary of the people around me lest I want to incur a murderous chase across the city streets.

Terrorising helpless NPCs is fun, but only for a short while.

I have a theory as to why players are pushing back against aggressive NPCs: they just don't like having to put in the effort after years of being able to do whatever they want in GTA Online. There's certainly some that will look back on the mostly timid NPCs of Los Santos and miss when all they had to do to steal a car was swing open its door and throw the limp driver out. Aside from shouting, there wasn't really anything a regular NPC could do to pose a threat to you back then.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Rockstar amped up the mayhem and carnage you could cause, turning it into a chaotic playground with few repercussions. GTA Online players have become accustomed to walking around like some vengeful god, wreaking havoc wherever or whenever they see fit, and only very occasionally dealing out mercy. Now these fickle deities have been forced to become human again.

A part of me understands the appeal. Terrorising helpless NPCs is fun, but only for a short while. NPCs that actually have a backbone offer an experience that will keep me interested for far longer.

Plus, Leonida is based on Florida, do you honestly think you could terrorise the streets of Miami or Tampa Bay and walk out completely unscathed? Yeah, I thought as much.

#3940. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#3938. Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

From a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

It makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

Thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

In terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make new, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

#3937. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.

"And then Obsidian was like, 'we'll try'"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

BioWare made one of the most beloved RPGs of all time with Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, but it was Obisidan that followed up with Knights of the Old Republic 2: The Sith Lords, another massively popular game. It's somewhat well-documented that publisher LucasArts wanted the sequel done quickly and that BioWare turned down the project for that reason, but in a new interview, BioWare veteran John Winski confirms that's the case and even puts an exact number on LucasArts' request.

Talking to Pembridge TV, Winski says LucasArts approached BioWare to develop Knights of the Old Republic 2 and asked for the project to be completed in just 18 months. "When LucasArts came to us and said, 'hey, you want to make a sequel?' We were like, 'OK,' and they gave us 18 months, and we were like, 'nope. No. We can't do it in 18 months. That's not enough time'," says Winski. "And then Obsidian was like, 'we'll try.'"

Try, Obsidian did, and for the most part, it succeeded. Winski rightfully points out Knights of the Old Republic 2 was released in a pretty sorry state, or in his words, not "totally finished," but he acknowledges that "a lot of people really love it" despite an "unreasonable" development cycle set by LucasArts. "It's still something that is worth having been done," he adds.

It really is remarkable how successful Obsidian was in following up such a celebrated release, and the very first RPG adaptation of Star Wars, with a game almost equally as beloved, all under pressure from the rights holder to deliver in an incredibly short timeframe. Just a couple of years later, the studio managed a similar feat with the release of Neverwinter Nights 2, yet another acclaimed RPG sequel to a BioWare-developed title. Leave it to Obsidian, I suppose.

#3935. I Hate Video Game Romance – Here's Why Grand Theft Auto VI Is The Exception

Generally speaking, I do not like romance mechanics in video games. I never find them convincing. Relationships build way too quickly, and usually all it takes to win someone over in an RPG or farming sim is a couple of conversations and a few gifts. In Grand Theft Auto VI, however, I'm extremely invested in the romance between Jason and Lucia, and it comes down to the game's quieter moments and slice-of-life mechanics.

If you've played Baldur's Gate 3, Stardew Valley, Date Everything, or practically any other game with romance options, you're familiar with the gameplay loop. I ask an NPC about her hometown, sympathize with her tragic backstory, promise to be there for her, and then give her the book, cake, or mining resource she likes. Do it enough, and one day she'll approach me with the uncharacteristically heartfelt confession that she can't stop thinking about me. The process is too transparently mechanical: I can scan the dialogue options and instantly know which of the three sentences will boost my affinity rating the most. It feels less like an actual relationship and more like a long-term scheme to program someone into dating.

Many games structured like the ones above are written as well as they can be. The issue is scope and structure. Romantic relationships are nuanced and unique, but there often aren't enough resources during a game's development to represent more than the basic building blocks. Players are meant to suspend disbelief and fill in the gaps – even though you technically only spoke to that villager a few dozen times, you're married with a child, so you imagine it's actually been years.

Of course, this scope is the difference between Grand Theft Auto VI and these other games – Rockstar made time and space for everything in this world, and romance is no exception.

Since they're dating when the game begins, Jason and Lucia admittedly skip the courtship phase that many games focus on, but their relationship is still conditional and malleable – if you want them to like each other, you should be acting in their best interests. And while the mechanical aspect of their romance is still plenty visible, the actions to increase that meter are vastly expanded. There has been a lot of discussion about the early game, when you can prep for Lucia's release from prison by buying flowers or groceries, and while I like those gestures, they're not what sold me on the relationship. Say what you will about modern dating standards, but flowers and food are too easy – too obvious for me to feel connected to and invested in a couple.

When I played this section, I felt like Jason's hair looked a little unkempt, so I got a shave and a haircut. And, to my surprise, this improved his relationship with Lucia. She wasn't around and wouldn't see the results until later, but it still scored me partner points, as did repairing the roof, painting the bedroom walls, and even giving Jason's car a new paint job. These unexpected, specific tasks don't just fill up the relationship gauge – they communicate information about both characters. Lucia is really looking forward to getting out of prison, and having a finished house and a clean, put-together partner sets her in a better mood. Meanwhile, my actions establish that my version of Jason knows she likes these things and would do them without even asking.

Minor, specific tasks like these are romantic because they imply a degree of thoughtfulness that sidesteps the grand gestures expected of a long-awaited reunion. Yes, there should be apples in the fridge, but that's a basic need; knowing the exact conditions Lucia wants the house to be in makes me believe Jason actually knows her. It becomes even more effective – both in real relationships and in the credibility of the in-game partnership – when thoughtfulness is demonstrated on a day-to-day basis, in the quiet moments.

Grand Theft Auto VI is a long game with a slow, steady pace, leaving room for the intimate interactions other games wouldn't have time for. If you come home at the end of the day and see your partner watching TV, you can sit next to them and get a bonus. When they go to sleep, they'll call out to you and ask you to lie in bed and scroll on your phone with them. You can hold hands in public, buy each other clothes, and remember to text back promptly. There are large, dramatic moments and professions of love, yes, but players are likely to experience vastly more of these minor interactions than those scripted cutscenes.

Romance can be flashy, but it has to be more than that. It's nice to see the starring duo dance, drive, and shoot at foes during cutscenes. But it's the long car rides when Lucia reassures Jason that her mom likes him, or the evening on the couch when Jason talks about how he likes the way Lucia laughs, that make this relationship work narratively.

What are your favorite video game romances? Let us know in the comments!

#3934. Unity launches new Fellowship program, offering a "no recoup" $50,000 grant to indie developers planning to launch their game in the next 12 months

Unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that plan release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the company has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental issues.

Unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

The grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

#3933. Marathon launch player numbers are about half those of the Server Slam, at least on PC

Marathon hasn't quite been able to attract the same volume of players the recent Server Slam did.

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially launched. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually showed up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

In Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

Marathon has now officially launched, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

Indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

#3932. Rockstar Reportedly Shopping Around Red Dead Redemption TV/Movie Rights, But Has Rejected Grand Theft Auto Adaptation Offers

Grand Theft Auto VI hasn't even been out for a week, and yet it's shattering records left and right, following in the footsteps of its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V. Despite that, developer Rockstar Games has reportedly continued to reject Hollywood TV and film adaptation offers for the crime saga series, according to a report from The Ankler. However, the studio is reportedly more open to a TV or film adaptation of its cowboy western series, Red Dead Redemption, according to the same report.

The Ankler reports that Rockstar is looking at possible licensing deals for its long-running western shooter series, which received its last entry in 2018, Red Dead Redemption II, for as much as $100 million. There's heavy emphasis on "possible," though, as there is no confirmation that Rockstar has said yes to any of these offers thus far. It's very likely a TV or film adaptation might never come to fruition – it's common for studios to field offers like this, sometimes with serious intent and other times as a quick look at the ocean of possibilities, as it were.

That said, video game adaptations continue to grow more and more popular, especially compared to their humble beginnings in Super Mario Bros. (1993), DOOM, and Mortal Kombat. Franchises like Sega's Sonic the Hedgehog, CD Projekt Red's Cyberpunk 2077, renewed Super Mario Bros. and Mortal Kombat efforts, and others, including Street Fighter, Resident Evil, Fallout, and Castlevania, have found great success on streaming services and on silver screens. Given how beloved the narratives of Rockstar's Red Dead Redemption series are, it's not surprising that production studios are interested in adapting those stories for TV and movie theater screens.

In the meantime, players have plenty to experience from Rockstar via its latest release, Grand Theft Auto VI, which launched on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S last week on November 19. Speaking of that game, read Game Informer's Grand Theft Auto VI review to see why it's one of the greatest games we've ever played, and check out the patch notes for the game's first update.

Four years ago (oh my god) strategy RPG Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga rather impressed our reviewer Jon Bolding. He wrote that "novel tactical mechanics make this indie a contender for the best strategy RPG this year".

Well, buckle up, 2027, because Symphony of War 2 has broken cover with a promise to release next year, and it's coming courtesy of the strategy sommeliers at publisher Hooded Horse, which I take as a very good sign.

SOW2 looks set to continue the Fire-Emblem-ish framework of its predecessor, tasking you with recruiting a gaggle of heroes to wage war with (and possibly compose symphonies, who's to say?) in "a world filled with political intrigue, betrayal, and tense, large-scale tactical battles". Which is a lot like our world, really.

It all looks very nice indeed. In the announcement trailer, we get glimpses of its squad-based combat and anime cutscenes, and I am officially into both. The art is poppy and distinctive, at some point an age-of-sail warship transforms into some kind of German WW1 destroyer, and the overworld triggers the regions in my brain devoted to thinking about Heroes of Might and Magic. Check, check, and check.

"Anime cutscenes!?" I hear you cry. "That sounds like the kind of thing that bespeaks a dense tapestry of lore I'll need to get to grips with first!" Well, apparently not. I am informed by Symphony of War 2's Steam page that the devs have no expectation you know what a "Nephilim Saga" even is before you pick this game up. "Symphony of War 2 is a standalone experience set several generations after the events of the first game—it can be enjoyed without having played Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga". The game's tale of a fallen empire trying to un-fall can be enjoyed single-serve.

#3930. "Games are best made by people": The IWGB and other European unions publish joint manifesto calling on workers, employers and consumers to reject genAI

As part of a summit meeting in Manchester yesterday, the IWGB Game Workers union have joined up with other unions spanning the Republic of Ireland's GWUI, Germany's GDRT, Italy's FIOM-CGIL, France's STJV, and Spain's CSVI to publish a manifesto that aims to "bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce" for consumers, workers and publishers alike.

The manifesto states that "GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce," and suggests actions that can be taken by all to reduce harm done to the industry. The manifesto specifies the "severe harm to the environment, the destruction of communities and the exploitation of the Global South" as wider harms of the technology, but maintains its focus on the industry itself.

The effects of the technology on gamemakers, such as "directly and indirectly replacing workers", "worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout", and "a marked decline in junior positions in the industry" are listed as core harms to be avoided and fought against, with the manifesto also noting that it also "removes a sense of ownership from workers [...] the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers' stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them." As it states, "games are best made by people."

The manifesto goes on to explains the unions' stance that genAI is "sold to employers as an alternative to workers", and its "predisposition towards sycophancy and lack of real world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions." In addition, its nature as a tool built on the theft of stolen third-party data is highlighted as an inherent danger, and the so-called loophole in only training models on internal data is equally highlighted as resulting in employees and creators rarely being credited or compensated for their work that is fed into the machine. This issue also ties into the inherent implicit and explicit discrimination that exists in genAI content due to datasets' "intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities", which leads to "a homogenisation of culture."

As for action, the manifest recommends that workers should "avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible", "distance yourself from genAI usage", and "make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI", as well as, of course, to "organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat." Similarly, employers are recommended to "ensure that no worker is required to use genAI", and to "disallow the use of genAI in the company code of conduct, even for early stages of development." Finally, for consumers, it simply advises to "support games made without genAI", and to "be vocal about disliking genAI in games."

It's an incredibly clear and concise statement that calls to mind the statement made by a selection of IGF jurors on the state of genAI in the industry and their decision not to vote for any game that uses genAI in any capacity. As both of these statements are joined in saying, "we do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games; it is not inevitable."

#3929. Nioh 3 patch finally makes summons useful in boss fights, brings free armour for everyone

There's a new Nioh 3 patch out in the wild, and it's one that any player who regularly summons in boss fights will really appreciate.

Team Ninja continues to work on Nioh 3. The developer has been releasing regular updates for the action RPG since its launch in early February. Earlier patches have addressed major bugs like healing item use inconsistencies, and more have arrived since to tackle various balance and loot-related issues.

Today’s patch, version 1.04, is a major one, coming in at well over 1GB. There’s plenty here worth getting excited about, so let’s dig in.

To begin with, this is the patch that adds the promised free armour sets for both Ninja, and Samurai. When Nioh 3 reached one million sales, Team Ninja said it would gift every player the Thunderous set in celebration, and the set’s two variants are now available in-game.

The more interesting side of the patch is, unsurprisingly, its change log. There appears to be a focus on online co-op and AI summons in this one, with various tweaks to the make the process more rewarding, and, in some cases, worthwhile.

The amount of Glory obtained when you complete a mission in multiplayer has been increased, regardless of which player was the host. The other major change mainly affects AI Benevolent Grave summons, making it so bosses will no longer target a single player for almost the entirety of the fight.

While summoning AI helpers has always been useful in Nioh 3, they didn’t always help in boss fights, specifically because the boss tended to focus on the player who summoned them, leaving the AI to run around eating AoE hits before dying.

Patch 1.04 makes a couple of welcome gameplay tweaks to the feel of combat. Ninjutsu, and Onmyo Magic will now hit their targets more consistently in situations where there’s a difference in elevation between the player and the enemy.

In the same vein, you’ll now be able to attack (quick/strong) right after jumping, which removes the pause that previously buffered the attack instead. This could mean even more air combos that don’t specifically require Martial Arts.

You can look forward to a couple of quality of life tweaks in this patch, too, such as the change that allows the game to automatically send any Sudama Soul Cores dropped by merchants to your item box. This happens from the second one onwards, which means you won’t have to pick half a dozen each time you go to sell a batch of items.

Speaking of the item box, the limit of forging materials has been increased for some of them. If you’ve been running Battle Scroll missions and Expeditions for gear, you’ll be happy to know that you can now exit the session from the main menu directly.

There’s plenty more to patch 1.04, including fixes and balance tweaks for several weapons, such as Samurai dual swords, odachi, and more for a few Ninja weapons, too. The patch also brings several bug fixes to the game.

You can read the full set of patch notes on Steam.

#3926. The Sims 4 patch makes it so your public lot gatherings won't be interrupted by rogue Sims

Stranger Sims will no longer just crash your public lot events in The Sims 4 to talk about whatever.

The Sims 4 will soon get a new update to resolve a number of issues, some of which have long caused headaches for players. The latest update will arrive March 17 on PC and Mac, followed by PlayStation and Xbox at an unspecified time later.

Outside of the fixes themselves, the patch also makes good on the recent re-commitment to continue improving quality of life for players, so there’s plenty here longtime players will appreciate.

In the latest episode of The Sims 4’s Laundry List blog series, where the developer goes through the most reported problems with the game and how it plans to solve them, we got a rundown of what to expect from next week’s patch.

You can look forward to five major fixes in this one, but arguably the most important is a change to how Sims determine who they speak with on a lot. This is especially relevant for public lots, where Sims would sometimes interrupt ongoing conversations by barging in and starting a conversation with your Sim.

Going forward, Sims will prioritise familiar Sims with whom they already have rapport, and be less likely to latch onto strangers. If you’ve witnessed a date your Sim was on get interrupted because of that, you’ll certainly appreciate the change.

Speaking of budding romance, Prom is coming back to in-game Calendars, and Sims can once again attend. Maxis said this will work with new and existing saves, and that you should also expect Prom goals to be completable once again.

Pets and animals get some love in this patch, too. First, pets and horses will no longer get lost in Premade Households. The fix prevents that from happening in new saves, but if you already had that happen to you in your current save, it’ll still be there.

You may now also assign animals to an Animal Shed after moving your house to a new lot, so you hopefully won’t be confused as to why they’re stuck in your inventory. This fix applies to existing saves as well as new ones.

Lower down the list of urgent fixes is an update that makes it so Sims’ eye blinking will show fully closed eyes for most interactions. The upcoming patch also comes with a host of Sims autonomy fixes, including one that prevents them from excessively flirting with each other.

Catch up on the full list at the link near the top of the page. And, in case you missed it, Maxis recently announced that The Sims 4 will soon get paid mods, something that many in the community are skeptical about.

#3925. I'm not saying Sleeping Dogs is the world's best life of crime sim, but no other game has replicated the importance of pork buns to whole manhood as deftly

For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again. The United Front Games-developed, Square Enix-published open-world crime romp is still as good as it’s always been, and still occupies its own corner in the dingy bar where the GTAs and GTA-likes hang out. Back in 2015, RPS co-founderman Alec Meer (RPS in peace) referred to it as “the halfway house between GTA's sneering arrogance and Saints Row's chaotic nonchalance”. Fair enough, I’ve never been that big a Saints Row guy, but I see slumbering canines a bit differently.

Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did. GTA 5 is an exotic and sun-kissed heist movie, a mould that GTA 6’s tale of gun-toting love in Vice City very much looks to follow. That leaves Sleeping Dogs protagonist Wei Shen standing next to Niko Bellic. One might be kicking faces in Hong Kong and the other might be getting into shootouts in New York, but both are fresh off the boat in places both familiar and alien. They find themselves caught between two lives.

For Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop. For Niko, it’s a balancing act between trying to settle old scores and start a fresh life in post 9/11 America. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a pork bun to chow down on. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a hotdog to chow down on. Both of their games are beloved for delivering tales which get the player invested in Wei and Niko specifically, that excel in putting you into the emotional shoes of these two underworld operators whose worlds are tearing at them from multiple angles as they claw their way to the top of the food chain.

Despite my headline gag, they do this with a comparably minimal amount of in-depth life-simmy details, like those that’re baked into Red Dead Redemption 2 (and GTA 6, to a degree) as some of the main selling points. Wei can buy a pork bun, the vendor loudly informs him that by doing so he’s avoiding the possibility of never becoming a whole man, but there’s no ‘whole manliness’ meter which demands to be satiated with regular pork bun munching, lest Wei become a less than whole man. All it does is give him a temporary health regeneration boost, because as we all know, the first thing the doctors do if you’re admitted to hospital with grievous wounds after a fight is serve you a scrumptious meal that miraculously closes up your cuts in minutes.

Sleeping Dogs dedicates all of its life simming effort to making you feel the weight of Wei’s torment as he grapples with an unsustainable double life of sinning and saintly acts. Like GTA 4, it’s not got the time, tech, or budget to adorn itself with animations or systems that replicate every aspect of Wei’s day-to-day existence in excruciating detail. It’s simply assumed, rather than demonstrated, that some of the back alleys he wanders down to bust drug dealers probably smell a bit unpleasant. He doesn’t have over 60 species of bird to catalogue as he commutes from North Point to the businessman-infested Central district, then on to the houseboat-heavy Aberdeen and gated communities of Kennedy Town. Though, he does keep nicking jade statues, in order to persuade his kung fu instructor to teach him some fun new ways to knee baddies into submission.

He can sing his lungs out to nail I Fought the Law at one of Hong Kong’s few karaoke booths or lose all of his cash playing mahjong, but he doesn’t have an endless laundry list of optional hobbies long enough to suck players who aren’t even particularly trying to get distracted in for hundreds of hours.

Then again, if he wanders into his Central apartment, Wei can take a piss. In truth, I’d forgotten about this prior to my recent revisit, but it is a wonderfully simple feature that really emphasises how things’ve changed for games like these in the years since 2012. I press one button when the prompt pops up near the loo, and Wei unzips before dribbling a rather loud trickle into the bowl. Then, he’s done. I can get him to wash his hands if I wish, but no bladder meter has gone down and no dirtiness meter is being satiated by my scrubbing. If Wei doesn’t take regular whizzes, no NPCs comment that he’s looking a bit pained, and his walking animation doesn’t dynamically adjust to huddle his legs closer together.

You could ask what was even the point of animating Wei’s pissing if it’s a pointless and totally optional activity, outside of arguably doing a tiny bit of work in helping Shen be convincingly human (and it unquestionably being quite funny the first time you stumble across it). By looping what would once have been one-note button presses into systems that help them play a more active role in fleshing out the world and the routines of its inhabitants, uber-detailed games like GTA 6 - at their best - add an extra layer of definition to the tales and adventures they depict.

They often feel like the sort of game Sleeping Dogs might’ve been if it’d had their tech and its budget was the GDP of real world Hong Kong. The question is, when limitations like that don’t apply to the degree they once did, where the line lies between extra layers which tangibly deepen the player’s experience and overindulgent bloat?

Sleeping Dogs, despite working in its own takes on elements of GTA, Saints Row, and I’d argue RGG Studio’s earlier Like A Dragon/Yakuza entries, is an unquestionably lean and focused game. Less isn’t necessarily more, especially if you were to ask slumbering canines-loving teenage me, who would’ve bitten your hand off for Hong Kong to boast even a third of the extra features and activities GTA 6 and Red Dead 2 pack into their life of crime sims.

The latter two are games that wouldn’t have been possible to make, at least in a format the masses would be able to play, back in the era when Sleeping Dogs and GTA 4 represented what an open-world crime game typically looked like. They’ve eaten up what used to be the domain of arcade racers like Midnight Club and hunting sims to step closer to being something reminiscent of Better Than Life, the addictive VR everything game from the Red Dwarfverse, which takes over players’ lives by simulating a world where everything they want can play out in reality-mimicking detail.

They aim to be far, far more than what defined their predecessors, and to use that to appeal to an ever-expanding audience. What I’m intrigued to see, whenever I get my hands on Rockstar’s latest work, is whether those like me who come to it having recently played a game like Sleeping Dogs will find a game that feels like it’s being pulled in a million different directions, to the point that it loses something of what historically has been at the centre of its fundamental appeal.

Or, to put it another way: is there a point at which you’ve eaten so many pork buns in one sitting that you begin to stray away from the self-actualisation which steady consumption of them is known to facilitate?

#3923. Crimson Desert PC specs don't keep resolution and framerate targets a secret, and they don't use upscaling for everything either

Finally, a PC specification list that actually indicates resolution and framerate targets, and doesn't leave console players behind.

Crimson Desert is a little over one week away from release, and developer Pearl Abyss has delivered the official, final list of specs for the game. The twist is that the specs not only include useful information for PC players, they also cover similarly relevant details for console players, who traditionally don’t get mentioned in those reveals.

The specs are decently detailed, but more surprisingly - except for a single instance - they don’t include upscaling on PC, another thing games have gotten too comfortable using, even with their lowest specs.

On the official Crimson Desert website, developer Pearl Abyss has delivered a chunky post breaking down five different sets of PC requirements for the upcoming open-world action RPG. Each set indicates the graphics preset being used - and crucially, the resolution and framerate targets you can expect with each.

With the exception of the Minimum spec, all other presets do not appear to rely on upscaling of any kind. They do not say, however, whether ray tracing is being used with any of them, which is a feature that will throw all of those specs out of whack.

That same transparency also extends to non-PC platforms, which traditionally get few, if any, details about their own resolution and framerate targets. The console set of specs are extensive, just like PC, covering both PlayStation, and Xbox.

It’s granular enough to indicate which upscaling tech is being used, where applicable. This is relevant for owners of a PS5 Pro, a console that has access to Sony’s PSSR upscaling, alongside the standard AMD FSR tech the base console - and Xbox - use.

The developer has also revealed the base resolution for each mode across each console, and the resolution the image will be upscaled to using whichever tech is being utilised.

And, if you’re one of the five people who play games on Mac, you’ll be thrilled to know that the specs also include a section for Mac devices, split between the different Mac chips. The quality preset being used with each is not clear, however.

Finally, there's a set of specs for the Rog Xbox Ally, covering both the X and S models.

Crimson Desert arrives March 20 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. You can expect more coverage from us at release and beyond.

#3920. Former Dishonored designer joins the team on New Blood's Victorian immersive sim Gloomwood, with a new level and new weapons coming this year

Gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher New Blood Interactive's latest update post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

In addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by New Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

Other than these new hires, the update is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

The update is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but New Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

#3919. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with a decent selection of maps and modes

Battlefield 6's second-ever free trial, and the first in 2026, is upon us.

Battlefield Studios has announced that Battlefield 6 is going free to play for one week next week. Well, a portion of the game is, anyway, as part of a free trial that will include some of the game’s most popular modes and maps.

Though it does not encompass the entirety of the game, the free trial is fairly generous. Here’s what to expect.

For starters, the trial kicks off Tuesday, March 17 and will run until the following Tuesday, March 24. The trial will be accessible from Battlefield Redsec, the already free-to-play portion of the game.

Once downloaded, you’ll find a new Battlefield 6 Free Trial section in the main menu. Because Redsec and Battlefield 6 multiplayer share progression, if you played the former at any point, you’ll be able to pick up from where you left off.

The same is also true the other way around; if this is your first time with Battlefield 6, all your unlocks will carry over to the full version, as well as to Redsec if you decide stick with the free-to-play off-shoot.

Once it kicks off, you’ll find three playlists to choose from. Casual Breakthrough, All-out Warfare, and a third playlist showcasing the new Nightfall game mode and its associated map.

All-out Warfare is what you come to Battlefield for, and that playlist features Conquest, Breakthrough, as well as BF6’s newcomer Escalation - all large-scale, combined arms game modes. They will be playable across four maps. You get to play on two from Season 2: Contaminated, and Hagental Base, one from Season 1: Eastwood, and Mirak Valley from the base game.

Casual Breakthrough is based on a playlist that already exists in the core game, and it’s really designed as a nice on-ramp for new players. It also offers less intense gameplay, perfect for people grinding unlocks.

Casual Breakthrough is limited to just 16 real players (eight per team), with the rest filled up with bots. You earn the same amount of XP in those matches, except when you interact with bots, so killing a bot will net less than a human player. Outside of that, unlocks, Challenges and all other things that don’t depend on stat-tracking can be done within.

In the trial, the Casual Breakthrough playlist includes Hagental Base, Contaminated, and Eastwood.

The most interesting is the third playlist, in part because its content will also be available to owners of the full game for the first time right alongside free-to-play players. Nightfall is a playlist exclusive to the Hagental Base map.

This is a very small map, so the mode selection here is Team Deathmatch, Squad Deathmatch, and Domination. Under Nightfall conditions, lights across the entire map are turned off, so you’re going to have use your NVGs to be able to see. This is also a god opportunity to try out weapon attachments that specifically work under low-light conditions, which typically don’t get much use in multiplayer.

March 17 also marks the launch of the second stage of Battlefield 6’s Season 2, which comes with the aforementioned Nightfall content, as well as a big new update - so the timing works out nicely for everyone.

The leads of Leonida, the biggest and best-known effort to recreate GTA 6 on PC, have quit the project, although others are still trying to carry it on.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just a day after Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker Cyberleek released the executable for the near-complete Xbox build of the game they dropped on Friday, at least two of the leads of Leonida, the biggest and best-known effort to recompile it to run on PC, have called it quits—seemingly under pressure from Take-Two and Rockstar.

The release of the exe made the pirated Xbox build effectively complete, and that opened the door for recomp projects to do their thing—that is, to leverage AI to quickly whip up a version of the game that will run on PC. Some hackers estimated it could be done within a week; Shayder, one of the lead developers on the Leonida project, said on X that followers could "expect a lot of static recompilation work to be done soon."

In a separate message on the Leonida Discord, Shayder tempered expectations a bit, writing that "it will take at least a week" to come up with something playable on PC. During a subsequent livestream, however, the team was seemingly able to get the GTA 6 splash screen to come up on PC, although it crashed after that. It sure seemed like things were moving ahead quickly.

But then things began moving quickly in a different direction. "I quit guys. I’m sorry," NotRexed, apparently the head of the project, posted last night on X. "I really want to make cool stuff but every single time shit happens that I can’t control so I’m stepping away. Thank you everybody, especially in the discord that allowed me to have this opportunity."

Later, they added, "Last post from me. I wanna clear things up. Rockstar taking my server down was only part of the reason. Like I’ve said before, I’m a 15 year old kid. Managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on Discord. Goodbye."

In a reply post, NotRexed stated explicitly that "Rockstar shut the server down," and shared an image of the copyright violation notice he'd received from Discord.

Shayder, who had previously predicted rapid progress on the Leonida effort following the release of the Xbox executable, took a more direct approach and simply deleted all of their X posts.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

This isn't necessarily the end of work to bring GTA 6 (in a probably not-great state) to PC via AI. Other such projects are underway, and there also appears to be an effort to carry on with Leonida: The website remains up, with a new name attached as owner, and there's at least one Discord server dedicated to it, although it appears a little less focused at this point than the original Leonida server. A new Github repository (NotRexed also deleted that) has been set up: It's "a continuation of NotRexed's Leonida project," according to a note on the project, which adds that "development continues here with its full commit history."

The advent of AI greatly simplifies and speeds up the work of bringing console games to PC (as long as you're not too picky about the quality), and that makes life tougher for companies that want to keep a lid on such projects. Still, it's not surprising that Take-Two and Rockstar are going hard on it: In the past, Take-Two has moved aggressively to shut down GTA 5 mod projects, an effort that culminated in its acquisition of the biggest and best of them. I've reached out to Take-Two for more information on the takedown and will update if I receive a reply.

#3916. Embracer begin yet another round of layoffs at Crystal Dynamics, while they're still midway through development on two Tomb Raider games

Update: Studio confirms eight staff lost their jobs

Update 18/11: Crystal Dynamics have provided the following statement to RPS, confirming it cut eight staff members:

As initially reported by Vertical Slice (thanks, Chris!), the workforce of Tomb Raider studio Crystal Dynamics is being cut as part of a new set of layoffs by owners Embracer. As far as is currently known, those affected include senior game designer Joshua Mitchell, senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker, and UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards, all of whom shared news of their redunancies on LinkedIn. There may be more affected, but neither Crystal Dynamics nor Embracer have offered comments on the reduction of staff as yet.

This now marks the studio's fifth round of layoffs since Embracer acquired it in 2022, following cuts in March 2025, August 2025, November 2025, and March this year. This is a drastic amount even considering the current state of the industry, with layoffs seemingly happening several times a week, but unfortunately, this is par for the course for Embracer. Even still, it makes one wonder just how many staff are left at Crystal Dynamics by now. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis and Tomb Raider: Catalyst are still in production, so you'd hope that the studio won't be shuttered entirely.

According to Legacy of Atlantis' Steam page, generative AI has been used in the development of Legacy of Atlantis "to support some early exploration and temporary development content. Any AI-assisted assets were either replaced or refined by humans in order to maintain the creative and artistic vision of the development team." I would hope that this isn't a case of Embracer cutting staff in the misguided hope that they can just be replaced with the use of genAI, but who can say. Solidarity to those affected, who I hope can find new work soon.

#3915. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.1 livestream reveals a pared-back, four-week update as HoYo plays catch-up

Honkai: Star Rail will continue the Planarcadia story arc in Version 4.1, as the Star Rail Fest presents a new twist.

A new Honkai: Star Rail Special Program has concluded, which means some fresh news about the game’s upcoming major update. Version 4.1, unveiled today as Unraveled for Daybreak, is the action RPG’s next moment, kicking off on March 25.

Unraveled for Daybreak is the next chapter in the ongoing story of Planarcadia, with the Astra Express Crew now invited to a fan fest inspired by their own past journeys. The aptly named Star Rail Fest is ostensibly hosted to allow more of the citizens of Arcadia to experience the Trailblaze.

As everyone’s eyes is fixated on the grand Star Rail Fest, the Phantasmoon Games continue to be in full swing, as does the war with the Supplicants. Star Rail Fest is, however, the big focus of this update, in case it wasn't obvious.

The event is made up of three large-scale zones, each themed around past excursions of the Astral Express. You’ll get to explore the Belobog Zone, Xianzhou Luofu Zone, and Penacony Zone. Later on, you’ll also be able to visit Pearluxe Tower, the headquarters of Pearluxe Corp.

Each area will feature its own attractions, such as the balloon figures of Supreme Guardian Cocolia and the Destruction Engine, the duel against the Lord Ravager Phantylia at Scalegorge Waterscape, and the Pearluxe Tower’s Alloy King Pom-Pom model.

The hot new arrival is bumbling noirish detective Ashveil whom we've met in Version 4.0, and who becomes a playable character with this update. Ashveil is a 5-Star Lightning-Type character, on the Path of The Hunt. You’ll be able to pull for him throughout 4.1's runtime, which is slightly reduced at four weeks instead of the usual six, in order to rebalance the schedule after the extra-long Version 3.8.

In combat, Ashveil is capable of increasing Crit Damage of all allies. He can also mark an enemy as Bait, which reduces the Defence of all enemies on the field so long as this tag holds. If Ashveil uses his Skill on the baited target, he will deal extra Damage and regain Skill Points for the team.

Ashveil can bully that baited target even further by launching Hounding Pursuit. If any of his teammates attacks the Bait, he can further deliver a follow-up attack that gradually accumulates Gluttony for as long as he’s in combat. Gluttony can later be consumed to boost follow-up attack damage.

If he lands a kill, Ashveil continues to deal damage to the next enemy he attacks. That buff is transferred if that enemy is killed. Even in map exploration, Ashveil can be deadly, capable of inflicting Stunned upon enemies within a specific range.

Returning characters this patch will be Hyacine in the first half, and Boothill in the second half. Once again, due to the reduced runtime, their banner reruns will be slightly shorter than normal, at just two weeks each instead of three — so be sure to take that into account if you're planning on pulling for either of them.

Version 4.1 also adds the Wispae War Saga, a new activity where you can practice your leadership skills by commanding different types of Wispae Soldiers in the Graphia Academy. You can upgrade each one, use spell cards to alter their effects, and later face other champions. You ultimately want to play this to unlock new Wispae Companions, not to mention complete the challenges within.

Finally, Version 4.1 marks the start of a new Arcadian Chronicles phase in the Divergent Universe. You’ll be able to use Waypoint Pass cards to explore the different areas. HoYo is also bringing back Planar Fissure and Garden of Plenty with double rewards. And as ever, if you log in for at least seven days after downloading the new patch, you’ll earn 10 premium banner pulls.

#3914. Exoprimal, Capcom's Dinosaur Hero Shooter, Will Go Offline And Become Unplayable Next Year

Capcom has been on a truly generational run in recent years, but even their legendary lineup of games was bound to have a few stumbling points. Exoprimal is a prime example – the dinosaur-themed hero shooter was not a terrible game by any means, but it requires online play and hasn't managed to maintain much of a player base. Today, Capcom announced plans to sunset the game, rendering it unplayable by September of next year.

"Thank you so much for your continued use of Exoprimal," an announcement on the Exoprimal site reads. "We regret to announce that service for Exoprimal will be discontinued as of 8:00 PM (PDT) on Wednesday, September 29, 2027." The announcement goes on to specify that the game will "no longer be playable" after that date – Exoprimal is an online-only game which requires an internet connection, so once the servers are offline, that's it.

Between now and September 29, Capcom will bring Exoprimal down in stages. As of yesterday, players can no longer purchase a Survival Pass Premium Tier for seasons 1-4. On March 30, Exoprimal and all its DLC will be de-listed from stores, but software owners can still play it and/or re-download it. Finally, the game will fully shut down by September 29.

Any online-only game has a finite lifespan, but it's still sad to see them go. Many gamers are frustrated in recent years because it feels like they don't really own anything, whether it's a subscription-based product or a digital download that can be discontinued at a moment's notice. It's the primary cause of outrage behind PlayStation's decision to stop producing physical discs in 2028.

As for Exoprimal, our reviewer Marcus Stewart largely enjoyed his time with it, writing, "Exoprimal’s creative subversion of expectations impressed me in more ways than one, and its approach to telling a robust narrative within a multiplayer framework is an example I hope other titles study. I just hope it’s enough to keep the game from going extinct."

#3912. Grand Theft Auto VI’s Breakout Star is Cool Dog – Here’s How to Meet Them

Grand Theft Auto games are full of NPCs that make the world feel more real, or more alive, or more dangerous. But none of them accomplish what GTAVI’s Cool Dog has done in their small cameo in the game: Be both Cool and a Dog.

What’s that, you say? You’ve been through most of the game at this point and haven’t met anyone named Cool Dog? Well, let’s fix that.

Rockstar seems like it was afraid the player was going to get themselves far out to sea in the ocean, as the fictional Leonida resembles an island more than the real-life analogue of Florida, and not have a way to boat back. It was seemingly so afraid, in fact, that it put together a mechanic to rescue you if you get lost.

To make this happen purposely instead of organically, you must take a boat out into open waters and put yourself as far away from open islands or other boats as possible. I did this by opening fire on my own boat, and after the two or three times it exploded and killed me, I managed to just gently sink one instead. If you are far enough out with no land or ships for miles, you will know within seconds, as you should hear the sound of a jetski and barking around you.

And then you will then meet Cool Dog. If you target them with the dialogue button, their name will show as Cool Dog, and you can question them, and ultimately accept the free ride they are offering you as either Lucia or Jason.

Cool Dog drives the jetski near land every so often, so if you’re just looking to get back, you can hop off wherever and swim the rest of the way. If you let Cool Dog finish their journey, though, they will take you to a little island with a bunch of other still-cool-but-not-as-cool dogs. There, Lucia or Jason can play catch with them, pet the dogs, and get a cool pair of Wraparound Shades themselves from a treasure chest. Playing with the dogs for a while will also get them to dig up treasure for you on the island, which can range anywhere from disposable to useful.

Cool Dog leaves their jetski on the shore, so if you want to leave, you can drive it back. But I like to assume Cool Dog either finds a better one or just picks their jetski up wherever you leave it.

Cool Dog is likely based on Loosy, a Golden Retriever who went viral in May for riding a jet ski around Ft. Lauderdale, Florida. Maybe that’s why the game was delayed, so Rockstar could have time to implement this pivotal feature.
